items.title: Asus ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM Review
items.author: Bo Moore
items.content:
Asus already had one of IGN’s favorite on its hands with the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCDP, delivering a gorgeous OLED panel that could render 4K games at a zippy 240Hz or swap to 1080p for an even faster 480Hz. It’s still an excellent option on the market and made all the more affordable by its age. Now almost two years on, Asus has the ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM, a very similar monitor with a smaller 27-inch panel that gets some new display tech for slight visual refinement. Of course, newer tends to mean more expensive, and this model is set to come in at $1,199, putting it well ahead of other competing OLED displays like the earlier PG32UCDP, which was sitting at $859 at the time of writing, or the 1440p/500Hz MSI MAG 272QP QD-OLED X50 at $599. Let’s have a look at how it stacks up.

Asus didn’t leave much out when it designed the ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM. That said, it doesn’t have speakers, but you’ll find it checks boxes in just about every other department.

From the front, it looks like a fairly tame, cleanly-built gaming monitor with perhaps a bit of a gaudy stand thanks to the angular, gamery aesthetic and the LED bat signal of the ROG logo that it wants to splash onto your desktop day and night (this can be turned off, thankfully). If you want, you can swap for a VESA stand using an included adapter. The provided stand is plenty functional, though, offering the typical range of adjustments you’ll find on a high-end monitor. There’s also a slot in the neck of the stand for passing through cables, and where some monitor stands make it quite a squeeze to even get power and a single HDMI cable through this portal, the PG27UCWM provides plenty of room for multiple cables.

The PG27UCWM is ready for a lot of cables, too. You’ll find two HDMI 2.1 ports, a DisplayPort 2.1a port, and even a capable USB-C port that’ll take in video and send out up to 90 watts of power. There are two USB ports for passing data to a connected system, letting the monitor serve as a USB hub as well with a KVM switch so you can pass that connection to the USB-C link or a separate USB-B link. If you want to connect speakers, there’s a headphone jack, too.

Around back, the PG27UCWM spices things up a little. Rather than the classic black ABS plastic you’ll find on half the monitors in the world, the PG27UCWM opts for a transparent plastic that gives it something of a cyberpunk aesthetic. It may still feel like cheap plastic, but it looks damn good.

Another feature is a presence sensor that can help preserve the lifespan of the OLED panel by dimming it whenever you step away. I didn’t find it overly sensitive, so I wasn’t concerned it’d blink off while I’m in the middle of a game.

Adjusting settings in the monitor is easy with a joystick control for navigating menus and making selections. This sits just behind the presence sensor at the bottom edge of the display.

Then there’s the display itself. The ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM packs a 4K/240Hz display with HDR10 and Dolby Vision support, variable refresh rates down to 48Hz, and a setting that swaps the display to 1080p and cranks the max refresh rate up to 480Hz.

The display is glossy, which can hurt in a bright room, but it has a decent anti-reflection coating that at least cuts down on how bright reflections appear.

The Asus ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM proves its worth with strong performance in objective measurements. My colorimeter measured a wide color gamut with 100% coverage of sRGB, 89% coverage of AdobeRGB, and 97% coverage of DCI-P3 color spaces. The monitor delivers the color accurately with an average dE1976 of 1.04 and a max of 2.66, making this a solid option for creative work. The monitor achieved these results in its default Racing picture profile, but not all different settings will perform as well. The Scenery picture profile, for instance, had a bad color accuracy dE1976 average of over 10.

By default, the display ran a tame 147.6 nits that would be comfortable in a modestly lit room, and that comes alongside infinite contrast thanks to 0.0-nit black levels. This level came alongside a standard 2.2 gamma curve and a comfortable 6600K whitepoint. Bumping the brightness level to 100% raised the white level to 249.7 nits.

HDR is a specialty for this display. It may not go incredibly bright for a full screen in normal use, but it can bring out more light in HDR. I measured a 294.8-nit whitepoint for a full screen and a 519-nit whitepoint for a 10% window with the remaining screenspace blacked out. That could go higher still for smaller highlights, but required switching the monitor to its Adjustable HDR setting and raising the brightness to 100%. In those conditions, I measured a 4% window at 1,066 nits and a 1% window at 1,172 nits. Those high brightness levels can sag quickly, but for temporary, bright bursts of HDR highlights, they’ll dazzle.

Motion clarity is also exceptional. The monitor's support for a 240Hz refresh rate in 4K or 480Hz in 1080p combined with the ultra-fast pixel response time of OLED keeps details sharp in fast motion.

The Asus ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM’s panel is excellent for both work and play. OLED panels had already been shifting away from troublesome sub-pixel layouts that could show color fringing on fine detail and text or basically anywhere with a sharp edge. With the PG27UCWM, Asus incorporates a panel with an RGB strip sub-pixel arrangement, aligning with the sub-pixel arrangement of your typical monitors and thus avoiding the issue entirely. Working in text documents, watching movies, and playing games, I never spotted the color fringing that had impacted some earlier OLED display.

Even if it had the fringing, it might have been hard to spot since the 4K panel is stunningly sharp on a 27-inch screen. I didn’t find myself pixel peeping. The screen looks great for movies, which are sharp and really play up the contrast and color the panel can provide. If you pair the monitor with the right video source, you can even tap into Dolby Vision.

Gaming just makes things all the better. Getting to run at up to 240Hz even at 4K makes the ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM quite the sight, and for more competitive or fast-paced games, the option to drop down to 1080p and crank it up to 480Hz can come in clutch. I played through a chunk of Assassin’s Creed Shadows and enjoyed the sharp detail and potent contrast that brings the game world to life one day, and the next swapped over to 1080p so I could blitz through levels in Hades 2 and power through enemies in Trepang2. The monitor kept up with all the intense action and kept the details incredibly clear.

Switching modes is also simple. A single tap on a dedicated shortcut button switches between modes (a clear on-screen indicator of this happening would be helpful, though).

The 1080p resolution starts to hurt a little on the 27-inch panel, but you really only need to swap over when you are playing something that calls for more than 240fps, and in those cases, the pixels will generally be moving too fast to notice them individually.

Mark Knapp is a contributing freelancer for IGN covering everything electronics and gaming hardware. He has over 10 years of experience in the tech industry with bylines at PCMag, Reviewed, CNET, and more. Find Mark on Twitter

items.title: Halloween: The Game Review So Far
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
Plenty of things are terrifying about a man in a boiler suit creeping up behind you, but it's hard to be scared of Halloween: The Game's Michael Myers when he strolls around the neighborhood with all the urgency of a retiree on a golf course. Admittedly, my early experience with the latest asymmetrical survival horror based on a famous movie came without the obligatory day one patch, so everything I’ve seen so far comes with that giant, flashing caveat. But after several hours, my immediate reaction is that this just isn't ready. I would think it’s ready if it were labeled asan early access game, which it’s not. Clumsy, buggy, and often frustrating, Halloween: The Game seems in need of considerable polish and bug squishing.

Developer Illfonic is, of course, almost synonymous with asymmetrical horror at this point, if not quite able to break the stranglehold Behaviour Interactive has with Dead by Daylight. In keeping with the traditions of the genre, you either play on your own as the killer, Michael Myers, and rampage through the town, or you work with up to three other humans and a handful of AI companions to loot items and keep yourself alive long enough to find, open, and escape the streets of Haddonfield on Halloween night in 1978.

Because of Illfonic's back catalog, I came in with high expectations, and knowing Halloween creator John Carpenter was also involved sent them soaring even further. You'd think, with the best part of a decade's learning and all that asym trial and error behind it, Halloween: The Game would be the most polished of all Illfonic's games. But — so far at least — that just doesn't seem to be the case.

Animations are broken or missing completely. I've had hard crashes that sent me back to my PS5 dash, averaging at least one an hour. Combat is beyond janky — several times now, I've stabbed a player and had my weapon phase right through them. Often the sound gets messed up, so when I open a door to my , I hear it to my , which is hugely irritating given sound is to a stealth horror game. And on two occasions, a quick time event bugged out and trapped me in a broken animation, giving Myers all the time in the world to step up right behind me. That was just as much fun and not-at-all-frustrating as it sounds.

The NPC AI is also hysterically stupid. Once, playing as Myers, I (loudly) busted through a front door and found all three remaining NPCs in the same room, still standing at the same window. I had executed two before the remaining one decided it was time to make a run for it.

The NPC AI is hysterically stupid.

It's galling because there are some ideas here. I had a great time with The Texas Chain Saw Massacre's spin on asymmetrical horror back in 2023, but within it was clear no one wanted to play as Leatherface because it was so much easier — and considerably more fun — to clock up XP and escape as a survivor.

In Halloween: The Game, however, Illfonic seems to have really worked to balance the odds between killer and civilian, and Myers is a blast to play. Even though he never, ever runs, making it next to impossible to take out a player if they've seen you, his special abilities — snuffing out all the lights in the immediate area; jumping from shadow to shadow; detecting nearby players — help mitigate that deeply unsatisfactory walking speed, especially if you nail the timing. Plus, the execution mechanic is a neat shortcut if you manage to get close enough to… well, execute it. The death animations, if often out of sync, are brilliantly brutal, too, particularly if you manage to catch a civilian, by a window or next to an electric oven. (I'm sure there's more still to discover!)

Best of all, this isn't just four humans against one killer. As Myers, your job is to wipe the map clean of all survivors, human and NPC alike. As a civilian, you need to creep around the deliciously 70s-inspired maps — everything, from the cars to the decor to the rotary phones, is on point here, not to mention the fashion! — quietly warning NPCs and instructing them to either hide, follow you, or escape.

There are plenty of items to gather as you creep through residential homes, including offensive weapons, defensive tools, and a host of goodies to bolster the odds of getting out of there unscathed. You'll never be able to take Myers out completely — just like the movies, this is a dude who does not know how to take the hint and die — but you can temporarily immobilize him with the right timing and the right equipment.

That said, why do we have to sit and watch Myers finish killing off idiot NPCs if all the human players are already dead? You're given QTEs when spectating — I hate them; there are too many, they're too boring, and I there's occasionally an input delay — but it's so tedious, especially as the maps are pretty chunky and make hunting down one last survivor time-consuming.

And it just doesn't perform well. Even beyond the poor AI and broken QTEs, I experienced numerous crashes, rubberbanding, and framerate drops for no discernible reason. Characters sometimes walked three feet off the ground. Interacting with items is completely hit-or-miss — half the time you can pick stuff up or remove a chain with a bolt cutter; half the time you cannot. Oh, and sometimes you can open a door, step through it, lock it, and then find yourself back outside the front, unable to get back in.

Like I said, I need to play on the launch patch before finalizing my thoughts — but, generally speaking, a day one update is rarely a miracle fix for all of a review build’s issues. Still, I'll be back once I've spent some time on the live servers with both the single and multiplayer modes (so far the former has completely underwhelmed me — again, mostly due to idiotic NPCs). I'd also like to better understand how the card perk system works and experiment with all the civilians' passive abilities. For now, though, it's difficult to recommend Halloween: The Game to anyone other than a horror fan with a Michael Myers shrine in their home (now that's a scary thought) or those with deep, affection for asymmetrical games.

items.title: Fury of Dracula (5th Edition) Board Game Review
items.author: Jacob Kienlen
items.content:
For those familiar with either the Fantasy Flight Games’ 3rd or WizKids’ 4th editions, the 5th edition is largely the same but for everyone else, Fury of Dracula is a one-versus-many with one person playing as the count and up to four other players controlling the hunters. As I mentioned a moment ago, this is a hidden movement game, where Dracula will be moving around the map, placing cards face down noting where he is and was, leaving dangers in his wake, while the hunters try to trap and kill the vampire lord. Each round, consisting of a Day and Night phase, begins with the hunters moving, supplying themselves with tools and special event cards, purchasing travel tickets, or searching for their target. During the day, these actions are generally safer, while attempting to resupply invites potentially hazardous events that may help Dracula instead.

Dracula’s turn is a bit less eventful, but debatably more important. Once all the hunters have taken their nighttime actions, Dracula is then able to move to a new location, placing face down a new location card on their growing trail and an encounter card. These encounters, secret much like the locations themselves until a hunter uncovers them, may spawn enemies, create diversions and delays for the hunters, or worse. Should one of these ever move off the board, “maturing” as it’s referred to, the despair track will increase, putting Dracula that much closer to securing his victory!

Despite the rather simplistic nature of these fights, it also has led to some of the tensest moments in board games I’ve ever had.

Unlike other hidden movement games, such as Whitehall Mystery (another personal favorite of mine) that is purely a game of cat and mouse, Fury of Dracula incorporates a combat mechanism. During situations where the hunters have cornered Dracula, both sides pick a card from their hands, composed of moves or helpful items like holy bullets and pistols on the side of the hunters, and then flip them, then resolve their effects. Despite the rather simplistic nature of these fights, it also has led to some of the tensest moments in board games I’ve ever had. Moments when misreading my opponent led them to safety, or one especially board-flipping time when I expected Dracula, who being only one hit away from death, to flee, only to have him decide to bite and knock me out instead. A defeat that pushed the despair track past its end, and handing the win to Dracula. Utterly infuriating, but also one of the aspects of Fury of Dracula that sets it above many other hidden movement games for me.

In addition to redone artwork (more on that in a bit), this new fifth edition does offer a couple of optional new elements that can shake up the formula a bit for those Fury vets out there. First is the addition of a fifth hunter to pick from, Jonathan Harker, who previously had been relegated to just an ally card. Mr. Harker now can be picked to replace one of the other hunters, and has some powerful abilities that should certainly help the good guys out. He’s able to not only deal additional damage when hitting Dracula but also, similar to his wife Mina, can force him to announce if Jonathan is in an adjacent spot. While a neat addition, it also feels like a bit of a halfbaked attempt too. Unlike the other hunters, Mr. Harker doesn’t get his own unique event card, and instead can simply use the one made for the hunter that he replaces. The balance of the game also doesn’t quite feel like it’s been balanced for him, and I found that when both Harkers were on the board, with their tracking talents, it made for a decently harder time for Dracula. He’s a fun “sometimes” change, but I plan to stick with my normal squad for most games.

Fury of Dracula is typically a game that can take a surprising amount of time, with some games I’ve played lasting past the four hour mark, and the second new addition with 5th edition is a faster game mode that can cut that in half or more. This new faster variant removes a couple of cards and blocks off a couple of the regions of the map (damn that Black Plague) while setting the board state roughly around where it would be after a “week” (about a third of the way through), granting hunters some items to start, Dracula with some damage, despair up a bit, and a few other tweaks. By-and-large I found this new variant to be a solid choice and makes Fury of Dracula a much more viable option on a weeknight. The smaller region and other adjustments (such as the instantaneous water movement and removing the single value train tickets) can make things far more swinging where getting away and staying hidden as Dracula can be more challenging. Again, just like with Harker, it works, but I’m curious how much balance testing went into it.

As one would expect from a new edition of a game, it isn’t usually just the gameplay or mechanics that get a refresh, but the artwork too, and it’s here where the 5th edition sees its biggest departure. Not because the map changes (though the town of Whitby, which plays an important role in the story of Bram Stoker’s original Dracula novel, is finally included) but the aesthetic has changed. And it’s also here where I think the new edition takes a step backwards from the third and fourth editions.

With exception of Dracula’s location cards, the artwork for the event, encounter, item, and combat cards all have ditched the dramatic and detailed full color artwork of the earlier iterations in favor of what I would describe as drawings you may see in an old Victorian-era newspaper. These black-and-white illustrations work, but just don’t have the same impact, with some appearing, dare I say, even a bit corny? The “Dark Call” card for example, now features Dracula staring at the moon with a few bats in front of him, compared to earlier versions where he appears to be basking in the night with hordes of bats all around, against a stormy sky. Then there is the new “Misdirect” which basically makes him look like Batman from The Animated Series, as opposed to a mysterious man in a top hat, lurking in the fog. Hunter and Dracula character cards don’t fare much better either, with the portraits replaced with sepia-tinted photographs of the character. Which, now that I think about it, could you even take a picture of Dracula? I mean, vampires don’t have reflections in mirrors, so can you photograph them? Oh well, questions for another time.

items.title: Bucking Fastard Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
This review is based on a screening at the Venice Film Festival. Bucking Fastard does not have a release date yet.

Basing his film loosely on Yorkshire twins Freda and Greta Chaplin, who notoriously spoke and moved in sync, Werner Herzog unfurls a real-life tale of codependence into a unique episodic drama about sheltered adults entering society for the very first time. The result, Bucking Fastard, is strange and wistful, verging occasionally on the surreal — it’s fittingly dedicated to David Lynch in its opening titles — and though its final notes lack the intended impact, the result is fantastical and worthwhile.

A large part of this comes down to the challenge of casting and directing such an idiosyncratic endeavor. Sisters Kate and Rooney Mara have had parallel careers which finally collide in Herzog’s latest. They play Jean and Joan Holbrooke — respectively, though it rarely matters. When the movie begins, the American siblings (“We’re not twins, we’re sisters,” they clarify emphatically and in unison) are placed on trial in Ireland, where they were raised, for stalking and harassing their suave neighbor, Mr. Mulroney (Orlando Bloom), who they claim to be in love with married to after a number of eager threesomes. The stakes here are low — a restraining order rather than a criminal conviction — allowing the story to take on mischievous hues as their obsessions play out in flashbacks.

Two things become immediately clear during this opening act: one, that the Mara sisters are a delight to watch together, delivering overlapping or echoing dialogue interspersed with wry smiles and knowing looks at one another; two, that the Holbrookes have a tragically incomplete understanding of the world despite their attempts at sexual independence. They have an antiquated way of speaking, moving, and dressing, so much so that the movie’s time period is practically obscured. Freda and Greta’s own harassment trial was in the 1980s — the film’s title comes from a verbal slip they made together in court — so it’s easy to assume a similar setting on screen until the first iPhone appears some thirty minutes in (courtesy of a curious onlooker demanding a selfie once the sisters become local celebrities).

The real twins were the subjects of their, but Herzog, who actually met them, circumvents the need or desire to craft a traditional biography. Instead, he extrapolates the isolation and self-loathing that he imagines might have defined their adult lives, as a pair of women so in tune with one another that they could barely communicate with the outside world or function apart. He also imbues his fictitious stand-ins with a certain naïveté of which men throughout the movie threaten to take advantage, creating an imposing uncertainty whenever the sisters step outside. In male-dominated pop culture, twin girls and women tend to occupy either a scary or salacious place; think the twin ghosts from The Shining, or the pornographic fantasy of bedding two identical women. These ideas loom large over the Holbrookes, as Herzog has them unknowingly wrestle with these forces during mundane interactions with men who are either devious or paternalistic, and whose benevolence might just come with invisible strings. Doubt always looms, even if the sisters seldom feel it themselves.

They are, in a sense, alien — twin souls who have no one but each other since the world rejects them both. 

However, once the film moves on from their trial and follows their attempts at living alone — which is to say, just the two of them — it takes on a more subdued tone, and not without good reason. Bucking Fastard seldom delves into the details of their past, but instead reverse-engineers its drama from fleeting mentions of their complicated upbringing by parents we never see and who want little to do with them once their impish antics begin to encompass arson. The absence of real love and acceptance hovers over the Holbrookes, causing them to misunderstand their own feelings at every turn, even if what they feel is pure. They are, in a sense, alien — twin souls who have no one but each other since the world rejects them both.

The movie is at its most poignant once they move far away from society to the lush Irish countryside. Once the sisters visit their ailing aunt Louise (Marion O'Dwyer) and befriend her sweet, burdened neighbor, the elderly shepherd McFarlane (Brendan Conroy), Bucking Fastard presses pause on its whimsy so that Jean and Joan can more carefully reflect on what they want from humanity and what it gives them in return. The answer isn’t always kind, but this setting affords them poetic promises of escape via a local legend surrounding a nearby cave, which — although they don’t have the capacity to digest its fiction — sparks something deep within them.

The film has a bittersweet lust for life, which Herzog finds nestled in still and painterly scenes between his crowded fish-eye close ups and uncanny framing (the camera, fittingly, moves in sync with both his leads). And although its eventual abstractions don’t quite reach meaningful catharsis or enlightenment — if anything, it ends on a surprising downswing — Herzog’s gentle tragedy of two women cast out by the world veers between amusing and straightforwardly touching, like an adult fairy tale about yearning for connection.

items.title: Breath of the Wild's New Vinyl Box Set Is an Amazing Addition to My Zelda Collection
items.author: Logan Plant
items.content:
One key reason The Legend of Zelda is my favorite video game series is its rich history of fantastic music. Whether it’s listening to official soundtracks on the Nintendo Music app, discovering inspired fan remixes online (my favorite is the Zelda & Chill trilogy of albums by Mikel), or learning to play them myself on piano, themes from Hyrule are a constant part of my life.

I gravitate most towards soundtracks from classic 3D Zeldas like Twilight Princess and The Wind Waker, but have also always had a soft spot for the piano-forward, post-apocalyptic tones of Breath of the Wild’s score. Like so many elements of Breath of the Wild, its soundtrack upended longstanding series conventions, largely abandoning bombastic, distinct overworld themes in favor of soft, ambient, minimalistic keystrokes that lay a lonely foundation for Link’s adventure.

Because of this shift, Breath of the Wild’s soundtrack has become slightly underrated in a way. Even though much of its music is subdued (which I really like on its own), there are still plenty of fully orchestrated, sweeping themes that play during boss battles, town visits, and key moments with the four Champions. There’s enough music to fill double-sided LPs, which is exactly what Nintendo has done.

Nintendo partnered with video game record label Laced Records on two different versions of Breath of the Wild’s soundtrack on vinyl: a 2LP set with 34 tracks, and an 8LP box set that includes 130 tracks. Notably, this is the first-ever Nintendo soundtrack released on vinyl outside of Japan. Nintendo sent IGN a copy of the 8LP box set, and I’ve spent the last week listening to each disc and poring over the included artwork. I’m very impressed with how closely the quality and attention to detail in this collection match that of its source material.

I’m not an audiophile by any stretch, but I love the physicality of listening to records and have amassed a small collection over the last several years. That includes the Ace Attorney box set also released by Laced Records a few years ago, and soundtracks from some of my favorite games like Celeste, Astro Bot Rescue Mission, and several others. Compared to all of those, this Breath of the Wild box set is likely my favorite already. It stands out with its inner cardboard slipcase that slides out to reveal all eight LPs nestled in a triangular sleeve featuring my favorite Breath of the Wild art: Link climbing a mountain as the sun sets over Hyrule behind him.

Each disc is inside its own sleeve featuring a different piece of key art. These depictions are nothing new if you’ve followed Breath of the Wild merchandise for the last nine years, but their painterly style still looks very nice. The discs are white with alternating blue and gold splatter effects, but to be honest, I’ve always just preferred standard black vinyl (which is an option on another edition).

Of course, music is made to be listened to, and I love the way Nintendo curated each disc in this collection. All eight LPs revolve around a different theme: Disc 2’s A-side is dedicated to several overworld themes you hear while exploring on foot or horseback, while its B-side is all about combat, with the battle themes heard when facing minibosses or battles within Shrines. There’s a disc dedicated to each Divine Beast questline, with a selection of themes from the region’s respective Champion, town, and dungeon. Disc 1’s B-side is dedicated to Kass, featuring accordion-heavy melodies the traveling bard performs throughout Hyrule.

I love the way Nintendo curated each disc in this collection.

Another cool detail is that the art on the sleeve matches that disc’s theme: the overworld disc’s sleeve depicts Link standing with his horse about to set off, while the Rito Village disc features Link fighting Windblight Ganon high above the Divine Beast Vah Medoh. There was clearly a lot of thought put into how to arrange all of this music – that you can technically experience in any order in the game – into one coherent collection. Having thematically organized discs has made me even more attached to this soundtrack, and I’ve loved throwing each one on and reliving my time in Breath of the Wild’s Hyrule in this way. They sounded great, too: none of the discs were warped, and I only noticed surface noise on one or two sides out of 16 total.

The highest compliment I can give this box set is that I already preordered a copy for myself (the provided copy will head to the IGN office in Los Angeles to live alongside other Zelda memorabilia gathered over the last 30 years). It’s truly an enthusiast item only – all of this music is available on Nintendo’s own streaming app, and it’s – but I’m thrilled to add it to my Zelda collection, alongside coffee table books, figures, and games. I can’t speak to the cheaper double vinyl release that’s , but if this box set’s quality is any indication, I imagine that one is great, too. My only hope now is that Nintendo and Laced Records will team up again for a Tears of the Kingdom version, which has a soundtrack I’ve always liked even more than Breath of the Wild’s.

Logan Plant is the host of Nintendo Voice Chat and IGN's Senior Editor, Playlist and DB. The Legend of Zelda is his favorite video game franchise of all time, and he is patiently awaiting the day Nintendo announces a brand new F-Zero. You can find new episodes of NVC every Friday on the IGN Games YouTube channel, Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or your favorite podcast app.

items.title: NHL 27 Review
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
As it is with so many annual sports series, incremental change has been the name of the game for EA’s NHL franchise for quite some time now. Rather than attempting to drastically alter its foundations, developer EA Vancouver has largely focused on making small tweaks that aim to dial up the authenticity wherever possible. It’s a strategy that continues with NHL 27, an annual entry that mostly feels the same as it has in recent years. The actual hockey remains strong, and there are a handful of small but welcome changes to be found, but the familiar feeling of nearly everything else has otherwise worn thin.

There are no new modes to speak of this year. Staples like Franchise, Build a Pro, World of Chel, and HUT serve as the main options, alongside smaller modes like Ones and Threes, plus tournaments like the World Juniors. The familiarity from past entries even extends to the menus, which look exactly the same as they did in NHL 26. Everything looks so similar, in fact, that some people might think they booted up last year’s game by mistake. There’s an argument to be made for not fixing what isn’t broken, but when a sequel doesn’t look any different right from the start up screens, it feels like a bad sign – especially for a series that often gets critiqued for its lack of differentiation.

In 2024, EA Sports made the decision to move the NHL series exclusively to PS5 and Xbox Series X|S. In theory, moving away from the previous console generation should have resulted in prettier graphics, but NHL 27 continues to look stuck in the past. NHL 26 featured some weird areas where team logos would get cut off on specific screens, and while that problem has been resolved or at least lessened this year, there are a lot of other lingering graphical issues throughout.

For one thing, character models are still ugly, and that extends to both hockey personnel and fans in the stands. The crowds are filled with people that look and move like they did multiple console generations ago, and the heroes of the NHL only fare slightly better. Some players look better than others, but hockey helmets help disguise the rougher designs. The same can’t be said for veteran coaches that have spent decades in the league, who sometimes look like poorly recreated custom characters.

Crowds look and move like they did multiple console generations ago.

What’s frustrating about all this is that there are moments where NHL 27 does visually impress. The surface of the ice continues to look bright and inviting, even as it deteriorates and gets snowed up throughout the course of a game. There are also some nice little details that pop up in unexpected places – at one point while my player was sitting in the penalty box, I noticed several scratches along the surface of the glass, meant to resemble scrapes left by errant shots. For those that have spent a significant amount of time playing the real sport, these accents help things feel more realistic.

For NHL 27, EA Vancouver has also polished up the arenas, putting more effort into making them look closer to their real-world counterparts. If you’ve ever stepped foot in some of these locations, you can feel the authenticity. I’ve been to arenas like Key Bank Center, Benchmark International Arena, and Nationwide Arena, and their digital versions look and feel closer to the real thing than they have in the past. That’s thanks in part to the additional landmarks in each arena, as well as the accurate goal celebrations and Jumbotron videos. These details make NHL 27 feel like a proper celebration of the culture surrounding hockey.

To that end, there have also been big changes to the music selection. I enjoyed a lot of the tracks in NHL 26, but rather than highlighting newer artists that kind of fit with hockey’s themes, this year EA licensed popular tracks you’d be likely to hear when attending or watching games. That means the music selection can be a little older at times, but it feels way more appropriate. I’ve associated songs like Bush’s “Machinehead” and Blur’s “Song 2” with hockey since I was a kid, and these are songs that still get regular play during games. You’ll even hear hype songs that are specific to certain NHL teams, like a track the Dallas Stars commissioned for their 1999 Stanley Cup run (which was the year Brett Hull’s foot was definitely in the crease). There is even a little background on these song selections, as the menus no longer offer just the name of the song and artist, but also a team logo and a small blurb about its history with that club, or with hockey in general. These small lessons quickly proved to be one of my favorite new features.

In the decades since the NHL series began, EA Vancouver has refined its take on hockey to a point where it consistently feels fun and exciting, even if it is all familiar. The gameplay in NHL 27 is more of the same, but that core experience largely remains enjoyable as well. This formula doesn’t need to be rebuilt from the ground up, because it really does work. There’s depth and healthy learning curve, but also plenty of options to tailor the experience to match your skill level or even how much time you have to play. It gets the important elements of hockey right, from the speed and power of the players, to the immense satisfaction of scoring a big goal.

The addition of playbooks is one of the biggest on-ice changes.

While that was all true last year as well, the addition of playbooks is one of the biggest changes in terms of the on-ice action. The 32 real-life teams of the NHL have a lot of nuances that make them feel distinct from one another, and EA Vancouver has created specific playbooks to reflect that. When selecting a team, there’s now an option to use their assigned playbook, or to switch to one that better matches your own style. For example, if you find that the AI teammates on the Red Wings play too conservatively in the neutral zone, you can choose a playbook that encourages more aggression. Figuring out how these combinations work adds a bit more depth to the package, as well as increased strategy and opportunities for creativity.

Those that enjoy customization options like this have Be a Pro mode to lean on as well, which allows the creation of an original character that can be taken through an NHL career. I’ve often enjoyed this mode because it feels a lot closer to playing the actual sport of hockey; you’re not constantly switching between players on the ice, instead focusing on a single guy. Unfortunately, this is one of the modes most blatantly similar to NHL 26. Press conferences are pretty much unchanged, with the same groan-inducing questions meant to increase (or decrease) your brand and popularity with your fans, teammates, and the organization. Parts of this mode felt stale last year, and basically nothing has been done to breathe new life into it.

The commentary is one area where NHL 27 definitely feels stuck in the past, too. It’s never been particularly great, exacerbated by the fact that nothing feels tailored for the specific teams on the ice. The commentators often refer to checks as a “crunch,” and during one game against the AHL’s Syracuse Crunch, that exact phrase was used. It seemed like the perfect opportunity for some wordplay like “a perfect crunch from the Syracuse Crunch” – it wouldn’t be all that clever, but it would have at least made things sound distinct from all the other times I heard it. No such luck. And then there’s the fact that the exact same comments are made game after game. You can only hear about a “really exciting tilt” so many times before you contemplate shutting this banter off altogether.

It’s not just the audio commentary that’s kind of broken, either. Be a Pro mode shows news headlines between games based on your performance, and they regurgitate the same critiques ceaselessly. If your team wins a blow out but your custom character didn’t score, it’s a “rough night,” with an image of your player looking downtrodden. Even if that’s not a great night for the individual player, it doesn’t quite match what happened on the ice. Additionally, there seems to be even less variety in these headlines than there was in NHL 26.

There are lots of small elements that hurt the immersion in NHL 27. During one game in Be a Pro, I was being pressured to head to the bench late in the third period, but didn’t have a good opportunity to change up. A whistle stopped play with 1.5 seconds left in regulation, and I assumed I’d still be on the ice for this small leftover amount of time. Instead, I found my custom player sitting down for the next face off, which would never happen in a real hockey game. EA Vancouver may have put a lot of effort into making the arenas match their real-life counterparts, but the games that play out within them don’t always match that level of care. For example, home crowds will eventually turn on their team during a blowout, but it’s not immediate – that means you’ll sometimes see fans dancing and enjoying hype songs during an early 3-0 deficit like nothing is going wrong.

items.title: Star Trek: Strange New Worlds Recap and Review - The Worst Episode of the Season Still Manages to Give Pike Some of His Best Scenes Ever
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
Man, this episode. Five minutes into it, I was ready to tear it apart, but then it had to go and turn into an actual serious story about what is essentially the tragedy of Captain Pike’s life. And not just that, but how he is learning to accept the unfair circumstances of his situation and still be thankful for the moments of beauty and grace and family that he has been afforded in his time, however brief (or cosmically/paradoxically long) that time has been.

Which isn’t to say that I’m going to tear into this episode some, because it is mostly a waste of what precious little time we have left with Strange New Worlds. Yeah, it’s the “soap opera episode,” and man, at this point I don’t know who the showrunners think they’re aiming some of these stories at.

Rhys Darby is back as Trelane (although they still don’t quite refer to him that way onscreen), the Q-like (or should we just say Q at this point?) being who plagued the crew last season in “Wedding Bell Blues” and who, of course, will also eventually cause problems for the Enterprise when Captain Kirk is running things, as seen in episode “The Squire of Gothos” (where he was played by William Campbell). This time around, Trelane has forced the Enterprise crew to live out a soap opera – just like on the old tee-vee, dontcha know! – complete with overlit sets, awkward close-ups, ridiculous plot developments, and over-the-top acting.

So yeah, it’s yet another . This is just what this show is now, I guess, and while it’s cute for a few minutes, the soap opera approach is not sustainable for a full-length episode. Which is probably why the show has to switch back to being, you know, a normal Star Trek episode about 36 minutes in. And that’s what’s so frustrating about “Like Chronitons Through the Hourglass” – not that it’s a dumb soap opera riff, but that it’s actually got a great Captain Pike story hidden inside it, albeit one that’s under-serviced because of the dumb soap opera riff.

I’ve given Anson Mount some grief lately about playing Pike in a way that was diminishing the captain and his status as the leader of an entire starship full of officers and crew. But then he comes along and acts the hell out of this episode, which is ultimately about his ongoing sense of loss and grief – and his inability to deal with either, as has been hinted at earlier in the season – over the loss of his lover Marie Batel (Melanie Scrofano) in last season’s finale.

And it wasn’t just Marie that he lost, but also the life that he lived with her – a complete life, where they had a daughter named Juliet (played by Anna Mirodin) and eventually aged into their golden years, all in a mere moment’s time in regular reality. Mount brings it in full force here, as he finally sits with the ship’s counsellor (played by soap opera legend Deidre Hall, of Days of Our Lives fame) and confronts what he’s been through. His memories of his daughter who never existed, and yet exist – “I taught her to read” – are so touching not only because of the writing, but also thanks to how Mount handles the scene, and it all just further drives home what a wasted opportunity the prior 36 minutes had been.

“Like Chronitons Through the Hourglass” is further hampered by the inclusion of Trelane, who is nothing but a bystander when all is said and done, literally watching events unfold from a TV control room. He’s surprised when Juliet manifests as an evocation of Pike’s subconscious, and he has no bearing on how Pike deals with that situation. He’s just , presumably because co-showrunner Akiva Goldsman likes TOS, and that just isn’t enough, particularly when the character plays as nothing more than a lame imitation of the William Campbell original.

Questions and Notes from the Q Continuum:

  • For everyone annoyed – or just wondering – why Trelane keeps showing up in Captain Pike’s era when his apparent first encounter with the Enterprise doesn’t happen until the Captain Kirk era, let’s just keep in mind that Trelane/Q are capable of flitting around in time, and indeed, exist outside of time. So a first appearance isn’t necessarily a first appearance in this case.
  • Speaking of which, yes, the “Proctor” played by Diane L. Johnstone is wearing a variation of Q’s “judge” costume from TNG’s “Encounter at Farpoint.” Why? At this point for SNW, I guess the answer to such a question is “why not?”
  • Once we’ve clicked back into the “real world,” La’an (Christina Chong) and Spock (Ethan Peck) have a nice scene which sure plays like the kind of non-closure closure that a break-up often finishes on. La’an saw in Soap Opera Sybok a glimmer of the more human Spock that she perhaps needed when they were together, but the real Spock is more Vulcan than ever here, unable to process what La’an’s going through when she mentions how hard it’s been since things between them ended. It’s another sad and very well acted scene.
  • What’s the deal with Sybok? Last we knew, he was still out there, waiting for his chance to actually show up on Strange New Worlds after a brief, viewed-from-behind cameo . Getting an Ethan Peck evil twin version here is very whatever, even if it is imaginary, particularly since the expectation after that Season 1 episode was that we would eventually get to see young Spock and young Sybok onscreen together. And man, is the clock ticking on SNW now.
  • So the OG Enterprise have a ship’s counsellor!

items.title: Legion of Super-Heroes #1 Review: Can DC Revitalize Its Most Notoriously Convoluted Franchise?
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
In DC's vast catalog of superhero franchises, The Legion of Super-Heroes has always been arguably the toughest sell for casual readers. Part of that is the dorky Silver Age trappings that have persisted across the decades, but it's mostly down to the sheer size of the massive ensemble cast and the fact that the series is constantly being retooled and rebooted every few years. The very nature of DC's sliding time scale means the future is always in flux, and so we're constantly treated to a different take on this team of idealistic teen heroes.

That all being said, DC has been finding great success in revamping old properties with the DC All In/Next Level initiative, so it only makes sense that the Legion be given the same treatment. And while the prospect of rebooting this convoluted franchise yet again is a little tiresome, the results speak for themselves. This is an engaging and gorgeously rendered entry point into The Legion of Super-Heroes.

Not that fans should have expected any less, given the pedigree of the creative team. The new volume is written by Joshua Williamson, a writer who's been busy these last few years transforming Superman into one of the best monthly books on the stands. It's illustrated by Hayden Sherman, an artist so talented that they were responsible for two of the five books nominated for IGN's Best Comic Book or Original Graphic Novel of 2025 award. Backed up by colorist extraordinaire Tamra Bonvillain and master letterer Hassan Otsmane-Elhaou, it would be shocking if the book weren't a success out of the gate.

Williamson is able to cut through the noise and the convoluted Legion trappings to focus on a few key elements in issue #1. His script reinforces the idea of legacy, always a powerful theme in the DCU. The Legionnaires are a group carrying on a proud tradition that started the first time a young Clark Kent put on a costume and started saving lives. There's also a central murder mystery fueling the conflict in issue #1, one that helps give the plot a greater sense of urgency and reminds us that the future isn't necessarily going to play out the way we expect.

It also helps that Williamson and co. don't immediately bombard readers with the full Legion cast upfront, but instead introduce a handful of key players scattered on different worlds. The script still assumes some basic familiarity on the reader's part with the likes of Lightning Lad and Saturn Girl, but by the end, readers should have little trouble connecting with them and their collective desire to use their powers for the betterment of the galaxy.

It's a solid script that lays out the basics of the series nicely, but make no mistake, the art is the real selling point in Legion of Super-Heroes #1. It's hard not to resent this book on some level, simply because it threatens to pull Sherman away from Absolute Wonder Woman. But the Absolute Universe's loss is clearly the Legion's gain.

Where to start? Sherman's figure work is exquisite. The characters are full of life without being burdened by excessive amounts of detail - one of the hallmarks of their style. What the lines themselves don't fill in, Bonvillain's colors are there to flesh out and add depth. The character designs themselves are a real treat. Sherman reinterprets many of the classic Legion costumes, transforming them into 31st century fashion designs moreso than actual uniforms.

Sherman's page layouts are also a true visual feast. They constantly play with the format and structure of the page, creating collage-like layouts of panels that evoke the work of J.H. Williams III (terrific company to be in). The reader's eye is constantly pulled in different directions, but the storytelling always remains clean and clear. There are other visual flourishes worth pointing out, like the lettering that forms the trail of Lightning Lad's electric bike and the nonverbal thought balloons that convey Saturn Girl's psychic conversations. In both cases, I'm not sure how much is Sherman's doing and how much is Otsmane-Elhaou's, but it doesn't much matter in the end. This art team is fully in sync, and the book benefits tremendously from having such an elegant, warm, and visually dynamic look.

items.title: Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 Review So Far
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
Perhaps no movie was primed to be a video game more than Aliens. A bunch of marines with guns up against hordes of monstrous beasties? That’s a video game, baby. That was true for the first Aliens: Fireteam Elite, a game I enjoyed but didn’t stick with for too long, and it’s also true of its sequel, which freshens that returning structure up with things like an additional player and a new class. I’m not done with Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 yet (the joys of international travel to Gamescom, I reckon), but I’ve played enough to start laying down thoughts like one of my squadmates is spiriting for an objective and my words are covering fire. The short version is this: I’m having a good time with my friends, but I am curious how long we’ll want to play after the credits roll.

You don’t have to be familiar with the original to understand what’s up here: the USS Endeavor received a transmission from a very sick-looking woman named Dr. Pearce based on LV-558, a Weyland-Yutani mining colony overrun by Xenomorphs. The marines sent in Fireteam Banshee, an elite squad, to contain the situation. They’ve all gone missing. Your Marine has been transferred to the Endeavor to bring them home and figure out what the hell is going on.

The first game wasn’t huge on story, and it doesn’t bog down Fireteam Elite 2 either. Between missions, you’ll hang out on the Endeavor and chat with your squad. There’s Shipp, the Endeavor’s CO; Ko, your tough-as-nails, no-nonsense squad leader; Piper, an analyst who is new to boots-on-the-ground work and a little nervous as a result; Esther, the ship’s android; Raptor, your dropship pilot with terrible (and I do mean ) jokes; and Wrench, your mechanic/weapons specialist/shopkeeper who dispenses rad bird facts.

I enjoy the crew, even if you only really interact with them from the waist up in very “look at their face while they talk to you” scenes. My only qualm is that, because they’re mostly just the voice in your ear on missions, there’s not much room for camaraderie – and when there is, everyone’s… too nice? One of the best parts of Aliens is that the characters don’t always get along, and while I think it’s great that Ko roasts Raptor (and you), I wish these characters razzed each other a bit more. It adds flavor, you know?

The missions themselves are pretty standard fare for the genre.

Like its predecessor, Aliens Fireteam Elite 2 is a class-based, co-op-focused shooter. (You can play it solo, but you’ll be teamed up with The Alphabet Boys: CPU-controlled androids named Alpha, Beta, and Gamma.) You’ve got six classes to choose from, many of which have their own Aliens analogue. Duelist is Hicks; Marauder is Vasquez; Medic is Dietrich (there’s a deep cut for you); and so on. My favorite was the all-new Specialist, which allows you to combine the features of multiple classes. Say, for instance, you want the special abilities of the Machinist (their turret and floating bodyguard drone) but also like the Marauder’s smartgun, which is one of my early favorites. Well, the Specialist will let you do that. It’s rad. That’s not to say there’s no benefit to sticking with the traditional classes; they have modifiers and special abilities that you’ll only get by leveling that class. But if you want to do some tweaking, Specialist is your guy (or gal).

The missions themselves are pretty standard fare for the genre, but they are fun. Drop into a Weyland-Yutani nightmare, hunt for intel/break stuff/complete other objectives, kill some monstrosities, hold out until you can get out, and then get out. It’s a fun loop, especially with friends, and is set apart from other games like it by how many different kinds of Xenomorphs there are.

Runners go down quickly, so they’re probably not worth spending anything fancy or consumable on (like grenades or mines or special ammo) – but they come in big groups and they’re fast little buggers, so you can get overwhelmed quickly. Spitters like to sit back and shoot acid from afar. Then you have the big dudes: the Warriors who will pick you up and try to get you with their second mouth; the hit-and-run Drones (think the Alien from the original Alien) who leap from the shadows and retreat from fire; large red Xenos called Prowlers that pounce on you, and so on. Figuring out the right answer for everything while managing your limited resources is a lot of fun, and Fireteam Elite 2 isn’t scared to throw everything at you in the big moments.

If that wasn’t enough, certain missions also ask you to deal with Wey-Yu synthetics. These require a more methodical “take cover, approach carefully” strategy, where the Xenos will just have you running for your lives. It’s a nice change of pace.

Fireteam Elite 2 isn’t scared to throw everything at you in the big moments.

My favorite thing, aside from the happy brain chemicals released from acquiring the M41A1 Pulse Rifle used in the film (you start with a newer model) and the sound it makes, are decals. See, you can customize your armor, which is already cool, but you can also add decals that you can move, rotate, and resize. I like the dropship I’ve attached to my Pulse Rifle and the heartbeat monitor that I’ve slapped on my breastplate, but I’m still searching for Vasquez’s Adios because I want to slap it on my smartgun. Feels right, you know?So far, I’m quite enjoying my time with Fireteam Elite 2, even if it doesn’t reinvent the wheel. It’s best with three friends (the squad size is now four marines, up from the original’s three, so your usual squad can all play instead of one person being perpetually sad), but it’s solid enough solo. Let me get to the bottom of this round of Weyland-Yutani’s startlingly bad decisions, and I’ll have a score for you. So far, however, I can confirm that it is in fact a bug hunt.

items.title: Mayday Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
The 1980s were rife with buddy comedies, and Mayday fits neatly within that genre, with Ryan Reynolds and Kenneth Branagh playing a U.S. Navy pilot and an ex-KGB agent, respectively, who traverse planes, trains, and automobiles to escape Soviet Russia.

While many Hollywood movies of that era were rife with anti-Russian sentiment, from Red Dawn to Rambo III, writing-directing duo Jonathan Goldstein and John Francis Daley take a more Spies Like Us approach to the Cold War, serving up a sometimes amusing yet boisterously action-packed reflection on geopolitical tension.

Set in 1987, a year after the release of the cinematic jingoism that was Top Gun, the film features Reynolds as Lieutenant Troy Kelly, eagerly filling the shoes of Tom Cruise's Maverick, albeit with his brand of deadpan humor – a humor here that rarely colors outside the lines of what we've seen him do before. Troy goes rogue to save his wingman's faulty plane, claims to be the best pilot of his unit and loves that Top Gun's popularity means he can queue-jump his way into any club. He applies that ego and arrogance to his dim perception of Russia and its people. "You can't reform something that is fundamentally broken," he says frankly. "It's not a society, it's a prison… silence is complicity."

Soon he's enlisted for a covert mission to co-pilot a spy plane, the Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird, to capture images of missile silos 1,200 miles inside the Soviet border. Thanks to the opening, we already know the operation goes sideways. After a brief but effectively thrilling sky battle with Russian fighter pilots, the so-called "beast" of his plane becomes fiery debris on the floor of a snow-laden forest, with an injured Troy clocking a mysterious man approaching before he blacks out.

Reynolds treads familiar sarcastic territory, but Branagh's kooky yet formidable ex-KGB agent elevates their oddball dynamic.

Troy wakes up in the cabin of Nikolai Ustinov, or "Nick" as he prefers, and the first thing he sees is Cruise's face on a Top Gun poster pinned to the wall. American militarist propaganda has penetrated the Iron Curtain, and given the film's lack of definitive identification of the rogue nation, it's easy to understand why it's Nick's favorite film. This is Branagh's third Russian action role in recent memory, after playing Viktor Cherevin in Jack Ryan: Shadow Recruit and Andrei Sator in , so it's refreshing to see him put those years of vocal coaching to more heroic use.

His Russian Americophile is less an overtly eccentric counterpart to Reynolds' straight(er) man but one with an earnest, subtly quirky appreciation of American "democracy, culture and food." There's also a lack of bravado when he outmanoeuvres both Troy and, later, patrons of a bar, in some neatly executed fight sequences. Both scenes employ wide shots and minimal edits to rivetingly capture how formidable Nick's combat skills are, adding another layer to the Branagh character, whose kind face should not lead one to mistake him for a man to be trifled with.

The rest of the film functions as a road movie, tracking their journey across Russia to find a means of escape, now that they are both enemies of the state, while being hunted by KGB official Alexander Volkov (Marcin Dorociński). He's far less menacing than, say, Christoph Waltz's Hans Landa from Inglourious Basterds, but still functions as an intimidating antagonist. Yet as much as it offers up action set-pieces like a face-off with a train full of Russian soldiers and a car chase involving a nuclear transporter in central Moscow, what's most compelling is how the very idea of American exceptionalism is dismantled. By breaking bread with common folk who welcome them into his home, conversing with Nick's activist daughter Anna (Maria Bakalova) and learning of a government cover-up that affected him personally, both Troy's prejudices and worldview crumble.

That Bruce Springsteen's Born in the USA album is as much of a running reference as Top Gun enriches the film's thematic core. Maybe it would have been too on-the-nose to include the record's eponymous anti-war song, but the fact that it's Nick's favourite cassette tape and one that Troy would prefer not to listen to for a 12-hour ride highlights the complexities and potential dysfunction of the American identity – as well as the universality of the Boss's love and lament for the working class. Borders and oceans might separate warring states, but the proletariat are very much the same: everyday people, suffering under government propaganda and class oppression.

Mayday doesn't get too deep in the weeds of political bureaucracy beyond what is required to push the plot forward, and perhaps its conclusion is a little too rosy. But that's Hollywood for you; idealism trumping reality so you can leave with a little more hope and understanding than despair.

items.title: The Paper Season 2 Review
items.author: Michael Peyton
items.content:
At the Toledo Truth Teller, love is in the air. And in a ditch. And at a gun range, on a podcast, and everywhere else you turn. In Season 2 of Peacock’s The Paper, the employees of the fictional Ohio-based newspaper are tangled up in so many office romances that it’s sometimes hard to keep track. The most recent batch of episodes of the Office spin-off puts relationships at the center, often to hilarious effect. It’s a season of television that swings for the fences, daring to explore what happens when you move beyond the classic “will they, won’t they” sitcom trope and dive into the actual consequences of workplace love affairs.

In Season 2, The Paper hangs nearly its entire narrative on the budding romance between competent, if often flailing, newspaper editor-in-chief Ned (Domhnall Gleeson) and star reporter Mare (Chelsea Frei). In the wake of the Season 1 finale, in which the staff of the Truth Teller swept the Ohio journalism awards, the two characters begin a secret office romance. From romantic getaways involving Orwellian food delivery carts to sweet FaceTime dinners, Ned and Mare often echo The Office’s Jim and Pam at their best. But whereas The Office’s central romance spent multiple seasons trapped in a cycle of yearning and missed opportunities, The Paper moves at a quicker pace. By the Season 2 premiere, Ned and Mare are fully together and enduring all the tribulations that come with a new relationship.

Nearly every episode of Season 2 centers around Ned and Mare’s romance intersecting in some (often hilariously) inconvenient way. Ned gets jealous when Mare (who’s ex-military) is a better shot than him when they visit a gun range to schmooze a local cop. They co-host a debate-style podcast where they manage to flirt and vehemently disagree at the same time. They cut short a romantic weekend away when the rest of the office can’t be trusted to handle an election-related story.

It’s a refreshing approach to sitcom relationships that shows the romantic progression between two characters who share the same passions (in this case, print journalism) and uses the relationship to make the workplace shenanigans more meaningful. That makes it all the more frustrating when Mare and Ned’s romance hits a predictable speed bump late in the season. I won’t spoil the blow-up here, but in typical TV comedy fashion, it involves miscommunication and a moldy muffin.

Similarly, the sheer volume of secondary characters who are involved in their own romantic entanglements (spanning everything from subtle flirtations to getting too close for comfort in a roadside ditch while a tornado passes overhead) can be overwhelming at times.

Resident attention seeker Esmeralda (the always-hilarious Sabrina Impacciatore) and corporate hack Ken (Tim Key) engage in a series of hijinks that frequently verge on a pseudo-relationship. Oscar (Oscar Martinez) concocts a scheme to snag a cute nursing home employee. Staffers Detrick (Melvin Gregg), Adelola (Gbemisola Ikumelo), Nicole (Ramona Young), and Troy (Eric Rahill) each deal with office crushes of their own. Even parent company CEO Marv (Allan Harvey) makes a play for love near the end of the season. Each of these storylines is benign enough on their own, but in aggregate, they risk turning The Paper from a cutting mockumentary about the state of journalism into a late-aughts romantic comedy with too many intersecting storylines.

Apart from the myriad romances, Season 2's most notable trait is the big comedic swings the show takes, moving beyond the small-ish comedy of The Office (golden tickets and rabies scares aside) into moments that are big, broad, and verging on farce. Yes, smart humor is still present (there’s a runner about newspaper tycoon William Randolph Hearst’s mistress that might be the funniest scene of the entire series), but Season 2 often pushes itself out of the confines of the mockumentary format into a show that’s more universal.

This sometimes doesn't work, like when, late in the season, Esmeralda goes “undercover,” Michael Scott-style, as a teenage boy to investigate her son’s school. But when the humor lands, it’s brilliant, like when Ned fakes a rat bite and nearly allows a pretend nurse to inject him with a giant syringe just to prove a point to Mare. Or when a secret office task force recreates a crime scene with condiments. It’s a scattershot approach that misses as often as it hits, but frequently fosters moments of pure comedic gold.

Beyond an expanded style of humor, The Paper adds a bevy of characters in Season 2 that enrich the world of the series. Chief among these is Lisa, the new wildly inappropriate HR representative, played by Lisa Gilroy. In a series of interactions with various Truth Teller employees, we see Lisa be competent, spiteful, manic, and hilariously bawdy. She’s the classic Office-universe character: decent at her job but somehow completely inept and infinitely watchable. Joining Gilroy this season are sitcom mainstay Andy Richter, playing a fleeting love interest for Esmeralda, and the legendary Jon Lovitz as a sandwich-loving new colleague. While the principal cast of The Paper is top-notch, these new additions fit perfectly into the series’ expanding scope.

Over the course of two seasons, The Paper has moved beyond its origins as an Office spin-off and created its own identity outside the walls of Dunder Mifflin. The Paper is at once more socially conscious (it is about under-resourced journalists, after all) and universal in its humor. But for fans of The Office, the seams of that series are still visible throughout The Paper, for better or for worse: A character spends the majority of the season away from their colleagues when they’re reassigned to another office (Dunder Mifflin Stamford, anyone?); Ned has his employees dress up like old-timey newspaper staff to celebrate the Truth Teller’s 125th anniversary; in a move right from the Dwight Schrute playbook, Nicole disguises herself as Lisa and stalks Detrick on a road trip after he shuns her romantic overtures; Esmeralda is seen in a very “Michael Klump”-esque fat suit.

The callbacks are obvious, welcome, and frustrating all at once. Given the pedigree of the team behind The Paper (the show was co-created by Office boss Greg Daniels and Office alums, including Matt Sohn, Dave Rogers, Jen Selotta, Ben Silverman, and Paul Lieberstein (Toby Flenderson himself!)), it’s understandable how The Paper brims with echoes of that beloved series. And while it’s occasionally fun to dive into the warm bath that is The Office nostalgia, The Paper has built up its own universe to such an extent that, after 20 episodes, the team behind it could probably stand to fully drive forward with their own gimmicks, archetypes, and inside jokes and leave Scranton, Pennsylvania in the dust.

items.title: Epomaker Split70 Keyboard Review
items.author: Bo Moore
items.content:
Unless you're a hardcore keyboard enthusiast, you might not know the difference between a 71-key keyboard and standard 100% or Tenkeyless (TKL) sizes. A 70% layout strips away the traditional number pad and the dedicated function row to achieve a much smaller desktop footprint. This size is popular because it saves desk space and keeps your mouse hand closer to your natural typing center, but it comes with a catch in that you're forced to rely on layered shortcut combinations to access the keys that were removed.

The Epomaker Split70 Keyboard takes this compact philosophy and physically cuts it in half, requiring you to connect the left and right sides with an included USB-C-to-USB-C cable. With this design, you can approximate something like a row-staggered Alice layout, but with a more traditional orientation by angling the two halves to perfectly match your natural shoulder width. It's a fantastic concept for ergonomics, but there's a steep learning curve that will undoubtedly change how you work.

Epomaker Split70 Keyboard – Customization and Design

The Epomaker Split70 comes in Black Grey and White Blue colorways, outfitted with gradient PBT Cherry-profile keycaps. In the box are the two keyboard halves, a USB-A to USB-C device-to-keyboard cable, a USB-C-to-USB-C cable to connect the left and right halves of the keyboard, a combination switch and keycap puller, three Macintosh keycaps to swap out, three extra Wisteria Linear Switch V2 switches, and paperwork.

I like the matte black plastic finish, but it does seem to accumulate light scratches through normal use. These scratches are only visible from certain angles, but once you see them, they can't be unseen. The left side of the keyboard features a built-in programmable volume knob, while there’s a cleverly hidden storage port on the back for the 2.4GHz wireless dongle.

Where the Split70 struggles is in its physical layout. Because the board is split and compact, Epomaker had to make some awkward compromises. The Tilde (~) key is pushed all the way to the right next to Backspace, there are two "B" keys to accommodate either hand, and the Escape key is shifted from its usual home. Most egregiously, the right Shift key is small, compressed to a standard 1U key size, and placed awkwardly to the left of the Up arrow. This placement took me quite a bit of time to get used to. I miss the Function and Home keys too. While you can access the Home key (like the other missing keys) via a shortcut (Fn + H in this case), there are practical limits to a keyboard with fewer keys. It's great to have the smaller size, but I'd happily give up a little width for frequently used keys rather than learning shortcut combinations.

Epomaker Split70 Keyboard – Performance and Software

Despite the layout gripes, typing on the Epomaker Split70 feels good. It comes equipped with Epomaker's Wisteria Linear V2 switches, which are pre-lubricated from the factory and require a light 45g of bottom-out force. However, if those aren't to your liking, the PCB is fully hot-swappable, allowing you to easily drop in your preferred 3-pin or 5-pin switches without any soldering. Combined with the gasket-mounted structure and a 5-layer sound-dampening system that features sandwiched latex, a PET sound-enhancement pad, and a silicone base, the keyboard absorbs hollow rattle and produces a smooth, creamy "thock" that any keyboard enthusiast can appreciate.

The tri-mode connectivity of Bluetooth 5.0, 2.4GHz, and Wired is powered by a 3,000mAh battery, providing more than 10 hours of usage with the RGB lights on, and up to several hundred hours with them off. To conserve battery life, the keyboard goes to sleep during inactivity, but it wakes up fast and gets right back to work. The south-facing RGB backlighting is vibrant, and the lighting gets really bright, even when set to just a fraction of its maximum capacity.

For gaming, the Split70 is nice and responsive for fast-paced games like , thanks to its 1000Hz polling rate in wired and 2.4GHz modes, which nets a low 3ms to 5ms latency. However, depending on key mapping, you'll likely still find that some keys are in a weird place during tense firefights until you’ve fully adjusted to its oddities.

As a nice gaming bonus, since all of the "smarts" and battery are contained on the left half of the keyboard, you can unplug the right half and put it aside. This allows you to use the left side independently, effectively turning it into a dedicated WASD macro pad, giving you a tremendous amount of free desk space on the right side for sweeping mouse movements.

The keyboard is compatible with the popular, open-source configuration application, VIA. By loading Epomaker's JSON file into the web-based app, you can easily remap the keys, assign custom macros, and tinker with the RGB settings to alleviate some of the layout frustrations.

Bill Loguidice is a contributing freelancer for IGN specializing in video game and computer hardware and accessories. He has several decades of experience and has written for a wide variety of publications. Bill has authored a dozen mass market books and was a writer and producer on a major feature film documentary on the history of video games.

items.title: LEGO Star Wars: The Mandalorian Review
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
LEGO Star Wars: The Mandalorian is essentially a tribute to/recap of all three seasons of the live-action series, along with for good measure. There’s some new material here in the form of a framing device involving Mando’s friends throwing him a party, but for the most part, this animated special focuses on having various characters recount Din (Gavin Hammon) and Grogu’s (David Acord) exploits with a suitably goofy LEGO flourish.

Why Disney didn’t release this special before The Mandalorian and Grogu hit theaters is beyond me. You’d think they’d want to throw their cowboy hat into the ring of the of the series, especially since this one has the benefit of being both so in-depth and so embellished. But, to be fair, The Mandalorian and Grogu is such an aggressively straightforward and simple film that no recap was ever really necessary in the first place.

In any case, fans of the series should get a kick out of seeing those events retold and distorted through the cutesy LEGO lens. This special is good for more than a few chuckles as it dives into the show’s big moments and lampoons them with loads of self-aware humor. And, as you’d expect, there’s no shortage of visual jokes to be found as the special takes full advantage of the fact that this is a universe where characters move like clunky toys and everything is constructed of plastic building blocks. It all makes for a silly and entertaining way to relive the original series.

It’s also amusing to note those characters and elements that get glossed over in the push to compress everything into a modest 45-minute runtime. Cara Dune is afforded neither an introduction nor any speaking lines, indicating what Lucasfilm’s current stance is on that particular embattled character. The special also glosses over much of The Mandalorian Season 3, which is probably for the best. Ultimately, LEGO Star Wars: The Mandalorian paints a very cohesive picture of Mando’s journey so far without getting too caught up in extraneous details. Exactly what you want out of a recap, in other words.

Adding to the fun is the fact that much of the live-action cast returns to voice their LEGO selves. The lineup includes Amy Sedaris’ Peli Motto, Bill Burr’s Miggs Mayfield, Temuera Morrison’s Boba Fett, Katee Sackhoff’s Bo-Katan Kryze, Rosario Dawson’s Ahsoka Tano, and Giancarlo Esposito’s Moff Gideon. Only Mando himself and a handful of other, minor characters have been recast.

The absence of Pedro Pascal in the voice cast is certainly disappointing, and probably the biggest knock against the special. Hammon is fine as the titular bounty hunter, but he doesn’t sound particularly close to Pascal. Luckily, it falls on the shoulders of other characters to actually narrate the extended flashbacks, so there’s plenty of room for Sedaris, Burr, and others to ham it up. Morrison’s Boba Fett also proves to be an unexpected highlight, as the special gives him an inflated sense of self-importance that the actor really runs with. Frankly, The Book of Boba Fett might have been a better show had it done the same.

LEGO Star Wars: The Mandalorian is cute and entertaining in equal measure. It even works as a nice little coda to the main series, highlighting how many friends and found family members Din Djarin has accumulated over the course of his adventures.

What it doesn’t do is blaze any new ground with the character. It’s hard not to wonder what might have been possible had this special focused on telling a wholly new and original story set within the world of The Mandalorian. Rather than recap adventures we’ve already seen, why not present a lost mission set during those gaps between seasons? Lucasfilm has really dropped the ball on that front over the years, with the promised Mandalorian spinoff novel never materializing and the tie-in comics also settling for adapting the series rather than expanding upon it. There’s room to dig deeper. But who knows? Perhaps this special will prove popular enough that we’ll get a proper LEGO Mandalorian spinoff. There’s certainly no shortage of potential there.

items.title: The Runner Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
If you’re looking for 84 minutes (with credits!) of Gal Gadot running through the streets of London in a desperate bid to save her son from a ruthless, anonymous villain, all while said baddie plays mind games with Gadot’s character via the true villain of the piece – the dreaded cellphone – then you’re in luck, because The Runner is on Prime Video now, just waiting for you to half pay attention while… scrolling through your feeds on your phone, probably.

The film stars the as Maia Marten, one of those super-powerful, super-smart, super-hot lawyers that movies and TV shows are always shoving at us. As the film starts, we learn that Maia has managed to nail down a key witness in the murder trial of a notorious crime boss. And now she’s being blackmailed by a mysterious “Caller,” as he’s called in the credits, to use her status as a super-powerful/super-smart/super-hot lawyer to get to that witness and murder him, thereby ensuring that the crime boss goes free. Easy peasy, right?

Using Maia’s kidnapped son Noah (Rory Wilmot) as the carrot the stick, the Caller forces our heroine to take on this job, but in one of The Runner’s several cracks in logic, for some reason he’s forcing her to do so on the clock, so she has to literally turn her morning run into a run for her son’s life, sprinting across London for most of the film and finding herself in increasingly dangerous and, at times, outlandish situations. (As soon as Maia mentions that Noah’s diabetic, in an awkward opening scene that is obviously all , we were clearly in for a Chekhov's Insulin situation.)

It’s hard not to like Gadot, no matter what role she’s playing, and she gives The Runner her all.

It’s hard not to like Gadot, no matter what role she’s playing – that fracas from a few years back notwithstanding – and she gives The Runner her all, even as she seems to be slowly running into permanent straight-to-streaming status. Certainly she sells Maia’s determination to save her son, as well as the character’s interior conflict regarding what she has to do in order to accomplish that first thing.
