Gadot does get an occasional laugh line, as she’s forced to do what the Caller says, even if that means calling a fellow mom who didn’t invite Noah to her kid’s birthday party a “bitch.” Meanwhile, an attempt at some back story complexity for Maia involving her own mother’s dark past doesn’t amount to much in the end, but that’s a failure of the script rather than the actress.

Nor does The Runner have a satisfying answer to how Maia can resolve her conundrum. “I’m not a killer,” she tells the Caller, and yet she must kill in order to save her boy. The film resorts to fairly ridiculous means to sort out this mess at its climax, which places it in the realm of something along the lines of an unsatisfying Columbo wrap-up as we’re told who did what when and how. Along the way, director Kevin Macdonald (Touching the Void, The Last King of Scotland) and scripter Mark Gibson seem to also be trying to comment on the state of the world today, a place where cellphones are ubiquitous and, I dunno, bad?

Macdonald does stage some engaging set pieces for Gadot as she constantly has to plow through pedestrians in order to get to her destination on time. Over the course of the film she finds herself running over bridges, onto boats, in front of cars, onto the London tube, over kiosks, and so on and so on. Intermixed with this action is flashes of the Caller, as well as the occasional voyeuristic glimpse of other folks in the city and what they’re saying and texting on their phones. As for the Caller himself, while he hacks into Maia’s phone and uses her most private information for his own ends, we never learn anything about him at all. That he’s played by Billions and Homeland’s Damian Lewis, even if the actor is mostly heard and rarely seen, makes this latter point all the more glaring, as he ultimately feels wasted in the role.

items.title: Orbitals Review
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
Orbitals sets out to carve its own space in the co-op-only genre. This bold adventure takes the joyous camaraderie of split-screen puzzle solving and couples it with a striking throwback anime visual style that captured my attention from the very first frame. The actual puzzling never reaches for new or daring ideas in the same way, mostly content to emulate its contemporaries with familiar concepts rather than push the limits of what's possible in cooperative games, which can make it a bit predictable at times. But exploring the unknown bounds of space with a partner is still an endearing romp that was well worth the 10 hours it took to reach the end.

Orbitals is solely a two-player experience, but thankfully it has both local and online play, as well as a friend pass that allows you to give someone else a copy that's only playable with the original owner; similar to what developer Hazelight does for games like It Takes Two and Split Fiction. This flexibility is good because everything in Orbitals is designed for two people, and the coordination many puzzles require is further emphasized by the fact that you're able to see your partner's side of the screen at all times, regardless of whether you play locally or online.

It makes a stunning first impression before you even get to that action, with a stylized player select menu that takes all of the charm of the early 90's anime you would see on Toonami and distills it into a nostalgia that felt tangible. Instantly, I was transported back to those late nights staying up past my bedtime in my parent's wood panelled basement to catch an episode of Cowboy Bebop or The 08th MS Team; a portal into a world I wouldn't come to fully understand until much later in life.

Orbitals thrives in its ability to evoke that era of animation, and attempts to push it one step further by thrusting you into the roles of two protagonists with fitting archetypes – Maki, a disorganized and somewhat blindly optimistic hero, and Omura, a slightly more put together and calculated counterpart. Together, they often feel like two sides of the same quirky and curious coin. These two often bounced off of each other; when Maki's high energy and over-the-top enthusiasm would start to take over, Omura would come in and rationalize a situation or further assess the problem. It brought a necessary balance to the dynamic, keeping everything in line.

It makes a stunning first impression before you even get to that action.

After their ship colony was nearly decimated by a powerful storm in space, both Maki and Omura were put into an I.M. – a machine that will reprint their bodies and keep their thoughts, emotions, and memories intact. Orbitals lightly touches on themes of what it means to be reprinted, with Omura making asides about if this is really him anymore after so many reprints, sometimes poking at these ideas philosophically but never fully wrestling with them. I wanted more from these ideas, especially as they come back around toward the end of Orbital's story, but they were never given time to fully flesh out that framework.

Tasked by your leader Togen to collect Cassettes that power your colony's ship, you'll venture out into the expanse. My partner and I started to delegate responsibilities as soon as we left our primary colony and headed for our travel ship. I helmed the main gun for the majority of our playthrough, blasting away any enemy ships or rockets that came within spitting distance. My partner in crime took the reigns of the ship itself, and he deftly drifted us through dangerous corridors, dashed out of the way of incoming attacks, and sometimes got us lost to the point where we struggled to make our way back on track.

The ship is the primary way of getting to your next objective. Orbitals is not an open world game, but it offers small pockets of freedom to fly around in. You'll fly to different rifts in the wall surrounding your colony to explore outside the bounds of charted territory. When you land in a new location, you're treated to big, bold text across the screen like you've loaded up the next episode in your VHS. You'll grab the highlighted weaponry from the center of the ship and head outside to a clearly marked hatch, and these hatches are where you find the more traditional action-adventure-style levels.

Early on, my partner and I explored a large mining operation run by robots with a knack for rhythm, which forced us to move to the beat as we looked for a Cassette in the deepest depths of mine shafts. We would pound in time with large drums, hop across moving platforms that swung side to side to the groove, and even found some form of alien life screaming along with the tune. These engaging moments mixed the world of Orbitals into the puzzle designs, making each puzzle feel contextually interesting and relevant as they fit with that rhythmic theme.

It teaches you the basics, then puts smart twists on those fundamentals.

Most puzzles put the focus on a few different weapons that are introduced early on. Rather than constantly reinventing the wheel in each new level, Orbitals teaches you the primary ways you will interact with the world around you and then puts smart twists on those fundamentals throughout. Each zone will often require two different gadgets that are stashed on your ship – these range from a laser beam that powers robots and guides drones to a grappling gun used to open panels and rotate platforms. My partner and I often took turns swapping between this simple yet effective arsenal of puzzle-solving tools, constantly trying to guess who would have the more interesting job once we reached a level and who would be relegated to moving platforms for the other person.

We solved a myriad of puzzles as we bounced from sector to sector – some were great, demanding teamwork or making us feel clever for having figured them out, while others felt more like we just stumbled into the answer rather than discerning a satisfying solution. More than once we were left scratching our heads wondering why something had worked, which speaks to a general lack of visual feedback. While many interactable objects are clearly marked with identifiable imagery, it's not always intuitive what Orbitals wants you to do with those pieces.

Some puzzles are as straightforward as having someone hook a yellow lever to pull down platforms for the other to jump and dash across, providing a simple yet effective way across chasm or dangerous terrain. Other puzzles are a bit more involved, such as trying to get a small platform around tight corners by simultaneously shifting your weight left and right while also using the grapple to slingshot yourself and get around even tighter turns.

Challenges like that are where Orbitals really shines – the tandem nature of these hurdles forced us to tighten up our communication even if we both thought we were Pacific Rim drift compatible. It required focus as we swirled around this seemingly never-ending maze of twists and turns, but once we locked in and got our methods airtight, we overcame the obstacle and improved our communication skills in the process.

Your ship goes from a means of transportation to a comfy and cozy home.

Introducing all of its base weapons upfront means you're exposed to fewer new mechanics as you get deeper in. As a consequence, Orbitals struggles to do anything transformative or with a final flourish toward the end. Two-thirds of the way through, I felt I had seen all of the tricks it had to offer, and an overeliance on its ship sections began to wear on me. While there were a few small surprises here and there, I spent the last three or so hours mostly going through the motions as I waited to see how it would wrap up. For how short of a game Orbitals is, it feels like it stumbles across the finish line with its final few sequences rather than taking a triumphant victory lap.

Despite that weak third act, Orbitals does a lot to make up for it in its smaller moments. As we walked around the ship interior in-between zones, it was fun to discover all of the new life that had stowed away. Capybaras, weird hi-fiving robots, and more began to breathe personality into our little vessel, making each journey to a new area exciting and filled with wonder as we waited to see who would choose to make this place their own next.

This cold hunk of steel went from nothing more than a means of transportation to a comfy and cozy home. As we explored more regions, we opened up new rooms onboard and found mini-games to compete in, complete with leaderboard spots to fight over. These rooms brightened up the space with ship combat simulators, electric jump ropes, and the kinds of diversions that made this world full of whimsy and intrigue.

The ship also contains smaller details that flesh out Omura and Maki as more well-rounded characters. Stumbling into Maki's disheveled and disorganized room with a drum set in the corner perfectly contrasts Omura's immaculately kept bedroom with a piano. The way they put their arms up when running down staircases, or how they interact with the many objects around the ship – these details inject personality into these characters outside of the main conversations and cutscenes. There is a curiosity throughout Orbitals, everything begging to be poked and prodded with an inquisitive nature.

I wanted more punch from a game inspired by the great anime that came before it.

Its story emulates some of the great plots of early 90's anime, but does little to rise above its inspirations or put its own stamp on these tales. Its early hours focus on the pressure put on Maki and Omura to travel beyond the broken colony, searching for machinery to keep their dwindling colony from extinctiown. It vaguely gestures at a larger conflict brewing, alluding to a dangerous storm approaching or differing ideologies on what it means to truly be alive, but it waits too long to meaningfully grapple with its more existential and interesting threads. I wanted to see more punch from a game so clearly inspired by a murderer's row of the great anime that came before it.

Despite its cooperative nature, this world can feel very isolating. You venture out into the great unknown and are sometimes met with deafening silence. Maki and Omura acknowledge that this silence could spell the end of their way of life, but rarely does Orbitals bring the stakes to match such a powerful concept. Instead, its main story hook relies heavily on gathering magical macguffins so Togen can put his plan into action. It doesn’t dwell on its self-reflective moments or give them room to breathe, swiftly ushering us from one level to the next with little reflection or examination as to how they all connect. It really is a story centered on Maki and Omura providing for their colony, and hoping to make everyone's lives better in the process – and while that’s enough to carry it across the finish line, it does fall short of the full potential it clearly has.

Whether we were on the ship or exploring an asteroid, all of Orbitals is carried by an eclectic soundtrack from artists like Swedish music duo Falk and Klou and Japanese singer-songwriter Mami Ayukawa. Its songs strike a balance between paying homage to anime of the 80's and 90's while finding its way to stand on its own. This soundtrack elevates everything around it without feeling like a backdrop just to set the scene – and the use of dynamic music that changes as you explore each zone gave them distinct personalities. It’s another tool in developer Shapefarm's belt to bring the vision of playable anime to life, and perhaps its most effective.

items.title: The Tower of Beggars: Stormfell Academy Book One Review
items.author: Jacob Kienlen
items.content:
When I first started reading Torsten Weitze's The Tower of Beggars, I was expecting something similar to the Harry Potter books. What I got instead was an entirely unique story filled with tales of gods and inequality. And while magic is a big part of this world, the first book in the series is true to its name and largely centers around a beggar's perspective. If you're looking for a good new fantasy series to dig into, I highly recommend checking it out.

The Tower of Beggars follows the story of Niri, a 16 year-old-girl with the kind of heritage that doesn't do her any favors. Her father was an Aeldae and her mother was a human, making her fully hated by any followers of the Crimson God throughout the Splinterlands. The hatred isn't unfounded; after all, the Aeldae had enslaved humans before the fall of their god, but that fact doesn't make Niri's life any easier. With both her parents dead, the story begins with her working as a coal girl for her mysterious nuncle (uncle) Vasdram, who seems to have a serious gambling problem.

The story starts out a bit slow as Niri's life as a coal girl sets up her beggar origins as well as the larger lore around the primary god, Malkar, who sets the rules of the land. It isn't until Niri is forced to leave her home and make use of Vasdram's Beggar Coin that the story truly gets going. Though I could argue that it really starts to become a fun read once Grabbasnack, the gold-eating pocket dragon, is introduced as a character in the first act.

As a protagonist, Niri is quite likable. She's smart, courageous, and tends to make the unselfish choice when it's presented to her. She's kind of the antithesis to the world she lives in, one which praises only selfishness and strength. Her biggest drawback as a character is that she is generally pretty weak and is constantly freezing up due to fear, which she calls "Sinking." If it weren't for the loyal companions she meets along the way, she'd clearly be dead in a hurry.

Overall, the story of The Tower of Beggars: Stormfell Academy Book One is quite good, but it wouldn't be nearly as enjoyable without the addition of the pocket dragon. Gh'rab-ehl-sh'naak (AKA Grabbasnack) is a tiny dragon who exclusively eats gold and can't keep his mouth shut. He's also an incredibly loyal friend and, after being freed from captivity by Niri, he becomes her first true steadfast companion. Thanks to his penchant for saying whatever he thinks at pretty much any moment, he keeps all of the dialogue feeling fresh when it could have run the risk of being too serious or stale. His constant search for gold to nibble on is also delightfully contradictory to the derelict environments Niri often finds herself in.

The delicate balance between surviving and actually finding time to learn is where this story really shines.

As for the actual magical school part of the story, it feels pretty light in the first book. While Niri does get admitted to the Stormfell Academy, she quickly finds that the Tower of Beggars isn't exactly a dedicated place of learning. She is only allowed to take a few different classes thanks to her Beggar Coin, but they are mostly designed for preparing lower-class citizens to become fodder for war. And despite free admittance to the academy, most of the folks in the Tower of Beggars are focused on finding riches (or just enough money to survive) in the monster-filled crater just outside of the academy.

The delicate balance between surviving and actually finding time to learn is where this story really shines. Niri has a fire to her, but she's ultimately weak and has the world working against her. Even though she's able to make it into the tower, she quickly finds that her admittance doesn't make her an equal by any means. The same prejudices that plagued her outside of the gates of Stormfell are only amplified by the cutthroat environment of the Tower of Beggars. The Crimson God himself promotes strength above all else, and Niri has to constantly struggle to make choices that will keep her alive without compromising her generous heart.

items.title: Onslaught Review
items.author: Tom Jorgensen
items.content:
will be released in theaters on September 4.

Onslaught is an apt title for Adam Wingard’s continuation of the world the director and co-writer Simon Barrett established early in their careers through You’re Next and The Guest, because it just never lets up. The platonic ideal of a “midnight movie,” Onslaught serves up heaping helpings of gruesome action, witty dialogue, Nazi experimentation, pro-veteran and anti-government sentiment, and three militarized Michael Myers figures hunting a community of unsuspecting trailer park residents. If all that sounds distasteful and exhausting to you, the rest of this review is not for you: you’re a lost cause and I invite you to go back to watching paint dry or whatever it is you do with your free time. For those with a taste for debaucherous mayhem in your cinema, pure and crazy… Onslaught, baby!

Over 92 rocket-powered minutes, Onslaught follows the classic “survive the night” story structure with a simple premise which Wingard imbues with all manner of schlocky adornment. At base level, Onslaught is about a trio of super-soldier experimentation subjects programmed to kill anyone in their path escaping containment and fulfilling their purpose in the desert community of Moriarty, New Mexico - the very same town at the heart of 2014’s The Guest. Onslaught finds a no-bullshit hero in Celeste (Adria Arjona), a veteran sniper struggling with PTSD and motherhood as she seeks peace at the Windy Oasis Trailer Park, where most of the movie’s back-half takes place. Celeste is quick to anger, but at least adept at directing those feelings in a constructive direction once the super-soldiers lay siege to her home. Across quiet character moments and very loud, raging action beats, Arjona carries the movie beautifully and it’s consistently fun watching her settle so easily into the action hero persona. Sarah Connor would be very proud.

With their painted faces, tactical gear and glowing eyes, the imposing trio driving Onslaught’s anarchy look like bosses that walked right out of Call of Duty’s Zombies mode. Even though they have cool codenames - The Crybaby, The Cockroach, The Butcher - there’s no discernable or relevant differences between the three once things go off the deep end. Since the action taking place at the trailer park is so narrowly focused, this is of little detriment to Onslaught, giving the characters multiple tough-to-beat foes to have to work their way through and allowing Wingard to stage cat-and-mouse games that start off especially chaotic when the trio is at full strength, and become more dread-inducing as the odds start to shift away from the trio of elite soldiers. Wingard does overplay his hand late in the game by attempting to use one of the super-soldiers as a thematic exclamation point long after Onslaught needs any more depths to plumb.

Stevens is always at his most interesting playing weirdos, and here, he swings for the campy fences and knocks one out of the park. 

It’s the fringes of Onslaught’s idiosyncratic world that really make you lean forward. Wingard’s The Guest and Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire collaborator Dan Stevens returns here as Dr. Kammler, a third-generation Nazi scientist with a penchant for white cloaks and being dominated by his wife, Frau Kammler (Rebecca Hall). Kammler can hardly contain his sensual glee at being on the precipice of delivering the Übermensch through his experimentations at a secret government base not far from the trailer park. Stevens is always at his most interesting playing weirdos, and here, he swings for the campy fences and knocks one out of the park.

Onslaught could have used more of Stevens’ off-beat performance to really shore up the “clean-up” efforts of the shadowy organization that produced the super-soldiers, but some of that sting is lessened by the other performers who shoulder that responsibility more as the story goes. Cyrus (Drew Starkey) is deployed to monitor the soldiers’ attack on the trailer park, and from the moment we meet him zonked out of his mind in a sex mansion, he manages to walk a fun tonal line of being both in over his head and completely in control at the same time. His most interesting material comes in his interactions with Frau Kammler, who winds up being one of Onslaught’s more interesting and enigmatic figures. The power dynamic between the elderly, milky-eyed Doctor Kammler and the much-younger Frau Kammler is intriguing to try and suss out, and only becomes more perplexing as Frau Kammler and Cyrus work with each other to maintain some level of operational control over the situation at the trailer park. Where Stevens aims for broad camp in his performance, Hall is much more restrained and lends Onslaught a lot of gravity.

Wingard’s most interesting thematic work comes through how this pack of freaks, whose aggression and sadomasochistic relationships with the intent to control are easily transposable onto any number of current events, something Onslaught crystallizes in its opening montage, which tracks the American government’s relationship to global war over the last 40 years.

Celeste isn’t alone in her fight against the test subjects, and the supporting cast at the trailer park counter the bizarre team of villains with down-home charm and no shortage of one-liners. Celeste’s main ally is Josiah (Reginald VelJohnson), himself a Vietnam War vet who, despite his ferocity and bravery once things go down, is quite gentle with Celeste as a mentor figure. That, of course, doesn’t stop VelJohnson from putting his Die Hard legacy to excellent use as a quip machine and sharpshooter in the fight against the soldiers.

Wingard also throws Eric Wareheim, he of Tim and Eric fame, into the mix as Kovacks, a sloppy Moriarty cop who knows nothing of either ferocity or bravery. Onslaught has no shortage of dark comedic energy, but Wareheim’s rhythm and ineptitude are always welcome and work well to cut especially tense moments. Celeste’s sharp edges are also well-rounded off by Daisy, her young daughter whose wealthy dad picks the worst weekend possible to dump her with mom. Daisy clearly spends most of her time in more civilized company, calling Celeste “ma’am” and doing chores around the house without being asked. Blake Kennedy, the young actor who plays Daisy, is a breath of fresh air and strikes the rare balance of naturalism and precociousness that never crosses the line into interminable “kid acting.” Daisy feels like a real, good egg and any time she’s in danger, it’s impossible not to care a little more about what’s going on, especially during one sequence where she has a real close call after being separated from Celeste.

Onslaught looks and sounds great, too. Oren Soffer’s cinematography does a fantastic job of highlighting the austere natural beauty of the Moriarty, New Mexico, setting, with blazing flames, kicked-up dust, and the warm glow of the trailer park’s lights giving the action a gritty, dirty feel that works to make that setting feel more real and not just gritty for gritty’s sake. Wingard lets the supernatural strength and resilience of the super-soldiers speak for itself, resisting the urge to get overly stylistic with how he stages the action and instead covering skirmishes with a more classical, straightforward approach that reinforces its ’80s action lineage, and these efforts are supported by a clear preference towards practical special effects throughout. Matt Pusti’s synthy score gives Onslaught a pulsing energy that really underlines the clear John Carpenter influence that Wingard is celebrating here, with simple repeating melodies that especially evoke two of Carpenter and Alan Howarth’s greatest scores: Escape from New York and Prince of Darkness.

items.title: The Blood of Dawnwalker Review
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
Ever since I first got infected with Porphyric Hemophilia in The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind or ran amok in Los Angeles in Vampire: The Masquerade – Bloodlines, I’ve been patiently waiting for an open-world vampire RPG that I could really sink my teeth into. Frustratingly, despite numerous attempts in all those years, I hadn’t found anything that quenched that long-standing thirst. With The Blood of Dawnwalker, an RPG that shares a ton of DNA with The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt made by some of its former developers, my hunt is finally over. Not only does it take the vampire fantasy to the neck-xt level, it also smartly finds workarounds for some of the limitations that can be a annoying (like having to stay out of the light), and introduces other interesting and clever ideas along the way. The day/night cycle that has you switching between human and vampire consistently makes for compelling questing, the limited time you’re given to complete your adventure makes even minor decisions carry enormous , and the numerous ways to make its bloody tale your own have motivated me to rise from the coffin and replay this journey more than any game has in quite a long time. This is the vampire RPG I’ve been waiting for and I find myself entirely under its spell.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is a third-person action RPG that puts you in the shoes of a no-longer-fully-human protagonist with long hair and facial scars who runs around using swords and magic to kill monsters in a gritty, dark fantasy setting. Perhaps not the most original premise from a bunch of former Witcher devs, but hey, if it ain’t broke, don’t pull it off the stuffed unicorn. You play as Coen of Laslea, whose town is taken over by vampires, then through a series of unfortunate events, is infected with vampirism and begins practicing the dark art of witchcraft on the same day. Tough break! Naturally, you set out on a roughly 40-hour quest for revenge against those evil bloodsuckers, using your unique abilities as a Dawnwalker (someone who has all the strengths and weaknesses of a vampire by night but a human by day) to save the valley of Vale Sangora from the clutches of evil.

While the premise is pretty basic, Dawnwalker excels in the telling, with a cast of extremely well-written characters across the board, a world that’s filled with more mysteries than you could ever hope to uncover during your time-constrained journey, and some weirdly impressive arguments for why maybe vampires be in charge of the world that made me pause to wonder if I was, in fact, the baddie. I instantly found myself eagerly spending time with Anca, the kind witch with a tragic past who split her time between either teaching me latin and magic or shamelessly flirting with me. Meanwhile, Crake, the rebel leader with a tendency to be heinously cruel in service of the cause, and Lacra, an allied vampire who casually committed war crimes half the time I hung out with her, managed to win me over despite being huge pains in my ass. Even the primary villains, like Brencis, who envisions a world ruled by vampires, and Ambrus, the footsoldier who revels in the displacement of the hierarchy of nobility and fancies a gentleman’s duel, were all incredibly compelling figures.

Dawnwalker’s best and most unique feature, quite appropriately for a game all about vampires, is its day/night cycle and the time mechanics built around it. As a spell-slinging human by day who turns into a blood-sucking monster by night, just about everything you do changes depending on the time of day. For example, in your human form you’ll guzzle down food and medicine to heal yourself, battle with swords and a fistful of witchcraft spells, and move around the old fashioned way by running, jumping, climbing, and whatnot. As a vampire, all that food and medicine is completely useless to you and your health can only be restored by consuming blood, plus you’ll primarily fight with your bare claws and gain a whole bunch of neat movement options – that includes teleporting around as a cloud of smoke, walking on walls and ceilings like the creepy little creature you are, and even turning into a wolf.

Dawnwalker’s best idea is its unique day/night cycle and time mechanics.

That means instead of building one loadout of armor, weapons, consumables, and abilities you’re happy with, Dawnwalker requires you to maintain two separate builds, which gave my stat-obsessed brain twice as much to joyfully tinker with. My vampire build was an absolute terror on the battlefield, with all my abilities centered around feeding off enemies to continually restore my health, and I sought out as many items as possible that increased my claw damage to turn myself into an unkillable unarmed freak of nature. Meanwhile, my human build primarily relied on high risk/high reward spells that put a whole bunch of nasty status effects on my foes at the cost of draining my own life and making me quite squishy. These two extremely different ways to play meant I was almost sitting forward during combat. Best of all, each of these loadouts is kept separate and automatically toggled between when you switch forms, so you don’t have to manually swap out all your armor and weapons twice a day.

Speaking of fighting, you’ll be doing quite a bit of that, since you’ll primarily solve your problems in Vale Sangora with the pointy end of your blade. The combat is quite good, with the caveat that it has a bit of a steep learning curve I suspect will be equally divisive. The main way in which it sets itself apart from most RPGs of this kind is that it uses a directional parry system where you have to match the direction the enemy is swinging, which kinda reminded me of For Honor. You can also just block attacks like normal, but doing so is fairly impractical (at least on higher difficulties) since it drains your stamina and doesn’t provide the openings for counterattacks that are so vital to success.

It sounds simple, but it took me longer than I’d like to admit to feel comfortable with it. The first handful of hours were fairly frustrating, and I frequently found myself fumbling through most combat encounters while cursing my ancestors. But there was light at the end of that tunnel – once I got over the hump and this system clicked, I grew to not only like it, but also feel pretty damn good at it. Now I’m able to down even the most formidable hordes without breaking a sweat, and that mastery felt earned beyond my stats going up. (Granted, I insist on playing most games on the hardest difficulty, so it’s quite possible I was just making things especially hard on myself and you’ll have an easier time from the jump.)

Aside from parrying, though, you’ll be using a pretty familiar bag of tricks for an action game like this, with a combination of standard attacks, special maneuvers that are specific to whichever weapon you’ve got equipped, and a bunch of abilities you can activate on a cooldown. Naturally, all of this will differ depending on whether or not you’re in human or vampire form, which goes a long way toward keeping things from getting too repetitive. For example, as a human, I fancied status effect spells that drained health and stunned enemies at the cost of my own life force, but as a vampire, I’d pummel things mercilessly with my bare hands and banshee shriek in my enemy’s face if I was feeling cheeky.

That said, these bouts definitely have some relatively minor but pretty obvious places they could improve. For example, the lock-on function consistently gave me trouble when trying to target a specific enemy, and it stayed annoying no matter how long I practiced with it. The camera could also get caught in odd spots in a way that was similarly aggravating. And while the variety of enemies you encounter is pretty good overall, the more common beasts you run into in the wild, like wolves and boars, appear way too frequently – by the end of my time with Coen, I was fully pissed off at the mere sight of the overpopulated canines.

Certain activities will change depending on when you choose to do them.

While adventuring out in the world, certain activities are only available at specific times of day. For example, you’ll need access to your vampire form’s superior movement capabilities in order to climb to the top of lookout towers and add nearby points of interest to your map, while rituals that require blood magic are only available in human form. But even activities available at any time, like most side quests, can have drastically different outcomes depending on which form you take. Some characters will be less likely to trust you if you interact with them in vampire form, while some areas might be inaccessible if you choose to tackle it while human. If you really muck things up, your character might just straight up murder a super important NPC because you stupidly interacted with them while in a state of overwhelming blood thirst. Not that I ever did that at all, because I’m super smart and very good at video games.

The most interesting aspect of The Blood of Dawnwalker’s day/night cycle is how it ties the passage of time to specific actions you take, giving you a finite amount of time to complete your overarching quest. After the story’s opening chapter, you’ll have exactly 30 days to bring Brencis’ rule to an end, and that deadline is stressfully enforced as almost every action you take costs a certain amount of time to complete. There isn’t a ticking timer or anything – in fact, you can freely explore the world or just stand around idly as long as you want without time passing. Instead, time is treated as a resource: want to buy the next level in a particular skill? Well, in addition to the skill points required, you’ll also have to pay the much more costly price of the hours it takes you to train in it. Want to help that old man with his minor problem because you’re roleplaying as a good person? Fine! Go right ahead… but that’s one fewer segment of time you’ve got to potentially complete a more substantial sidequest.

At first I thought I might find this limitation irritating, since I quite enjoy taking my time to smell the roses and mark every checkbox off my list in these kinds of open-worlds, but I quickly realized how treating time as a currency makes just about every aspect of Dawnwalker better. No matter how hard you try, you won’t have enough hours to complete every side quest, buy every skill, or tie up every loose end as well as you’d like, which means you’re forced to compromise, pick your battles, and make hard but impactful decisions almost constantly. For example, early on in my travels, I talked my way into a prison camp to get some intel from a prisoner there, one I would have gone out of my way to rescue under normal circumstances. But when I saw that it would cost me three pips of time to do so (each day has 16 total), I decided to leave him to rot instead. I was forced to make compromises like this every step of the way, all in service of ensuring I had enough time for the important stuff, and I regularly found myself surprised at my own decisions. Fittingly, it made me feel like I truly was letting the darkness of my new vampiric abilities compromise my humanity in my quest for revenge. It’s brutal, nerve-wracking, and completely awesome.

This harrowing time-crunch ultimately has a pretty enormous impact on how your journey ends as well. I won’t spoil anything, but alternate endings will only open up to you if you’ve met certain characters or taken specific actions. On my first playthrough, there were entire supporting characters and story components I completely missed out on, and I didn’t realize the scope of what I hadn’t seen until I took an entirely different approach on my second playthrough. In a third (much shorter) playthrough, I just went for a brute force approach to see what would happen if I rushed straight to the end without meeting anyone while leveling up as little as possible, and I was not disappointed by the hilarious result. This is one of those games where I not only wanted to play through multiple times, but it almost felt mandatory in order to see everything Vale Sangora had in store. I can’t remember the last time I’ve felt that way about an RPG.

One thing I often worry about with open-world RPGs is just how bad their performance and technical bugs might be, and The Blood of Dawnwalker thankfully finds itself on the less egregious side of the spectrum. Sure, on a standard PlayStation 5 it’s got the occasional framerate wonkiness, the camera sometimes clips through stuff in awkward ways, and an enemy will occasionally go right through the floor when you kill it – but almost everything I saw like that was pretty minor and uncommon, and I never had a single hard crash, broken questline, or anything else frustrating like that. The worst thing I encountered with regularity were blurry textures on characters’ clothes (or sometimes detail in their faces), which would distractingly never smooth out from time to time. Importantly, the version I played did not include the 60fps performance mode that was recently announced, so I can’t say just how well it holds up on that front, but I wasn’t particularly bothered by the 30FPS quality mode since it usually looked and ran well enough anyway.

items.title: Onimusha: Way of the Sword Review
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
For as long as I can remember, I have wanted to be perfect for 10 seconds. To write the perfect sentence. One that sings, captures hearts, evokes emotion. To make the perfect play, to eradicate the gap between body and mind and live a complete life in an instant of pure movement. To be, for just a moment, free. There are moments in Onimusha: Way of the Sword where everything else fades. The controller falls away, the universe collapses, and the distance between you and Miyamoto Musashi is annihilated. There is nothing but move and counter move, sword clashing against sword, call and response. You will risk everything for another moment, another chance, and do it again and again until you claim victory or your chances are spent. As long as Musashi stands, you have a chance. Onimusha challenged me, and I used it to challenge myself. I found a connection to its hero I did not expect and will carry with me. It is a remarkable video game.

Strange as it may seem, Onimusha is a work of very loose historical fiction. Miyamoto Musashi, and his rival Sasaki Ganryu, both based on real samurai who share their names, are attacked and killed by monsters called Genma after Musashi bests the master of a rival school of swordsmanship. A strange man in hell then brings Musashi back to life and forces him to wear an Oni gauntlet that can absorb the souls of fallen foes – one that already contains the spirit of a woman named Shizuka. Now imbued with the power to stand against the Genma, Shizuka has Musashi join forces with fellow Onimusha Takamura, who guards the Oni Gate separating Earth and hell, and his assistant Okuni, to protect the city from the corrupting Malice that’s twisting everything in sight. But Musashi isn’t the only one the old man gifts with a gauntlet. Ganryu gets one, too, and it can feed on human souls just as easily as Genma ones.

There’s more, but I really do think you should discover Way of the Sword’s story for yourself. It’s more of a character-driven tale than a plot-driven one, and this cast sings. At the center of it is Musashi, as compelling and outright cool a character as you could ask for. He resents the gauntlet and the strength it has given him because he didn’t earn it himself. He’s not a hero by nature; he just wants to hone his skill with a blade and prove himself against the best the world has to offer, but his circumstances have left him no other choice. The only way to get the gauntlet off is to feed it enough Genma souls that it heals him. He’s crude and his confidence can border on arrogance, but it’s part of what makes him so interesting. He can give as good as he gets with both his mouth and his sword, and it’s incredible to watch him talk mad smack to demons as he cuts them down in the coolest ways you’ve ever seen. There are cutscenes here that are so insanely well done they've seared themselves into my brain, and watching Musashi do his thing often had me and my wife (who became so invested in the story that she watched my entire playthrough) saying “Oh my God, he's so cool” out loud what felt like every five minutes.

But it's not just Musashi's skills and swagger that endears him to you, it’s also the relationships he forms with the other characters. Watching him go from calling Shizuka “Gauntlet Lady” to forming a ride-or-die partnership is a joy, and I understood it because I cared about her, too. Musashi is the kind of guy who is smart enough to respect and listen to Takamura and a good enough man to mentor Okuni where he can. These relationships form Onimusha's emotional core, and as I watched its characters change and come to care about one another, I did, too. It doesn’t hurt that Way of the Sword has some of the best facial animations I’ve ever seen in a video game, effectively selling every second of how they feel. Musashi’s is based on the likeness of legendary Japanese actor Toishiro Mifune, who played Musashi in films directed by the equally legendary Akira Kurosawa, and Capcom has done a remarkable job of translating aspects of Mifune's on-screen mannerisms, right down to his habit of scratching the back of his head and the way he walks. Using the likeness of a dead actor is always fraught, but Capcom navigates it with aplomb here.

Musashi is as compelling and outright cool a character as you could ask for.

Onimusha treats its characters with respect, but it's never scared to have fun with them, either. Musashi is a brilliant swordsman, but it’s hilarious to watch him get into a boat to help Okuni and realize he doesn't know how to steer it because he doesn't know what an oar is – something Okuni rightfully roasts him for. But he gives it right back when Okuni volunteers to play “the most beautiful girl” in a nearby village so they can use her as bait to sneak into a fortress.

And Shizuka… man. If Musashi is Onimusha’ heart, Shizuka is its clear-eyed, iron-willed soul. It would be easy for the spirit of a woman trapped in the Oni gauntlet to be reduced to a supporting character, there solely to make Musashi (and by extension, you) feel good about himself. And while she does gas you up when you pull off something impressive, she's never presented as anything less than Musashi's equal. He may be the one doing the fighting, but he can only do it because he's borrowing her strength. They need each other, and their journey is one they could only undertake together.

The writing is impressive, but what truly elevates Onimusha is its voice acting. I played Way of the Sword in Japanese, and the performances are incredible across the board. The English cast does fine work, too, but everyone sounds like they're from some part of London, and it distracted me – besides, playing a game set in feudal Japan in English seems just as wrong as watching Seven Samurai or Yojimbo dubbed. And after rolling credits, it is impossible for me to imagine anyone other than Yoshimasa Hosoya as Musashi or Aya Endō as Shizuka. If you can get past the subtitles, it’s absolutely how I recommend playing.

Onimusha isn’t just an excellent story; it’s also a damn fine action game. Since Takamura’s duty is to protect the hellgate, he can’t leave it alone for long, lest a bunch of Genma pour out. That leaves Musashi to take the fight to them. Kyoto serves as your base of operations, but it’s also the city you’re fighting to protect. You’ll spend much of your time here killing Genma, closing the Rifts that spawn them, and destroying the Malice-producing plants infesting the city, which opens up more of it for you to explore.

But you’re not stuck here; Musashi and Shizuka will also often visit other areas – temples, mountains, forests, and even the Imperial palace – to hunt down powerful Genma and try to figure out why everything is going sideways. These areas feel like real, distinct places, each with its own vibe. Onimusha is more “wheel and spokes” than open world, but there’s plenty to explore and discover, including materials that can be used to upgrade Musashi’s sword, clothing, and Oni Gauntlet, providing more damage, health, and souls (which fuel the gauntlet's power), respectively. Any trip into the wider world means fighting Genma, but fortunately, that’s where Onimusha is at its best.

Initially, I actually found it too easy, so I gave myself a challenge: I would play without using any items. That meant everything from healing items to items that brought me back from the dead to items that granted temporary buffs. I figured it wouldn’t last; you aren’t meant to play this way, so I thought eventually I’d grow bored of the self-imposed handicap, get stuck, or just need to get this review wrapped up. I came close to giving in many times, but I’d always think, “I’ve made it this far, just a few more tries and then I’ll give up.” But I never did, and eventually the credits rolled. I’m not telling you this to brag; I didn’t do it to put it in this review, or to show off, or prove a point. I did it because I wanted to see if I could. I did it for myself. And I can’t write about Onimusha without talking about it.

Onimusha isn’t just an excellent story; it’s also a damn fine action game.

Musashi is an incredibly skilled swordsman, with light and heavy attacks that he can chain together into short combos. It’s familiar stuff, but thankfully none of it (nor sprinting in combat) costs stamina. Musashi is always at his best. And where he (and Onimusha’s combat system) really shines is on defense. In addition to your standard block, Musashi can also dodge, parry, reflect, and do special Issen counterattacks if your timing is precise enough.

Each option has its own strengths and weaknesses. Dodging is the most reliable, but unless you perfectly time your move, it will only just get you out of trouble or allow for limited follow-up attacks. Parries require putting yourself in harm's way, but they both deplete a foe's stamina and open them up to further punishment, while deflects just take a massive chunk of stamina (unless you're returning a projectile to sender; that hurts). But the white whale is the Issen: by pressing an attack button at just the right time (in my experience, as soon as the enemy swings their weapon), Musashi will sidestep the blow so quickly it looks like he disappears and then reappears somewhere else, triggering a counterattack that deals massive damage and takes out an enormous chunk of stamina.

Landing this feels and if you time another attack as your Issen hits, you can chain them together to wipe out several small enemies at once. If you attack at the same moment an enemy does, you’ll even trigger a clash where you have to press the opposite button of the attack you started with to win (so if you trigger one using a light attack, you must follow up with a heavy). You might also lock swords and have to mash your way out to overpower your foe. All of these systems combine to form a combat system where you always have to pay attention, and anything feels like it can happen. It never gets old.

What makes Onimusha's combat special is that each move has its place. Blocking is a last resort as it depletes stamina. Run out, and an attack will break your guard and deal huge damage. But that doesn’t mean it doesn't have its uses in a pinch. Dodging is particularly good against unarmed attacks, and if you time one right, you’ll fill a special meter. Once full, a perfectly timed dodge – called a Reflex Dodge – will trigger a Reflex Combo, which will often kill smaller Genma outright and carve a chunk from elite enemies. Parries do a little of everything, and if you nail one, you charge the Blazing Gauge, which sets your sword aflame and boosts the damage of your attacks. Deflects sacrifice the parry’s ability for follow-up attacks in exchange for massive stamina damage, perfect against armored enemies who are largely immune to your basic attacks because you can focus on depleting their stamina entirely, staggering them, and landing the absurdly powerful Break Issen execution-style moves. But as powerful as deflects and parries are, they can’t be used against grabs, which require you to dodge.

The Issen is your defensive holy grail, but the timing is strict and it doesn’t work on everything: certain attacks can't be Issen’d but be dodged, parried, or deflected, forcing you to pick a strategy on the fly. But the biggest risk of the Issen is that it leaves you wide open – miss it, and you're eating whatever attack is coming your way. And since the telegraphed (and most damaging) attacks are the most reliable targets for Issen attempts, the technique always carries huge risks. But lock down your timing and you can do things like Issen a lightning bolt. Yes, really.

What’s most impressive, though, is how Way of the Sword sells all of this. When you parry or deflect an attack, it doesn’t look like you are just performing some generic animation; it looks like you parry that attack. It makes each fight, especially against bosses, feel like unique clashes between individuals. Feedback is everything in an action game like this, and few feel as good moment-to-moment as Onimusha does. Combine all that with your regular attacks, the special Oni Armaments that serve as high-damage-but-meter-dependent attacks, and the ability to break a foe's guard (plus a few other things I won't spoil), and Onimusha is constantly forcing you to both come up with a strong gameplan and react quickly as the unexpected tests it.

What makes combat special is how each move has its place.

Every enemy in Onimusha drops souls: yellow souls heal, red souls are currency used to upgrade certain skills, and blue souls recharge your Oni Armaments. There is another kind, but… well, you should see it for yourself. The only reliable way to get yellow souls is to use a certain Oni Armament (shout out to The Two Celestials) or pull off Break Issens. When you use a Break Issen on a regular foe, you kill them outright; against bosses, however, you choose a weak point to attack. Striking at weak points marked in red will deal incredible damage, while choosing a purple one will deal about half as much damage, but reward you with additional souls.

And here is where my own imposed limitations came into play most. By refusing to use healing items, I made it so I could only recover health by absorbing souls (or at the Spirit Mirrors where you save your game between fights). That meant staggering the boss or spending my limited gauge to use The Two Celestials. Success was built in small moments: knowing when to parry, when to deflect, when to risk the Issen, and managing my Reflex Dodges so I could spend Reflex Combos in the right moments. I had to truly learn the fights, to understand what was needed of me. Since many bosses have multiple phases and health bars, I would often master one only to get clobbered by the next. And every mistake cost me; getting hit by a powerful strike cost souls. I wasn't just losing health, I was being robbed of the resources I needed to get it back, too. And I wasn't the only one who could absorb souls – most bosses can as well, and if they get enough, they'll power up and gain access to new attacks that would normally be granted during the next phase, making the rest of the fight even harder. That rules.

Some fights took me hours to learn, and I was often tempted to give up. Onimusha wasn't doing this to me, I was doing it to myself – but each time I died, I would take a deep breath, wait a second, and press retry. To succeed required every tool I had. I couldn’t think beyond the next 10 seconds, the next decision, the next moment. Most Break Issens were spent to gain souls and restore my health. Each time, I was prolonging the fight. Each time, I was betting on myself for the next 10 seconds. I learned sometimes it was better to take the damage on the Break Issens when my health was in a good place, how to save The Two Celestials for the right moments.

After a while, the distance between myself and Musashi would fall away as I acted purely on instinct. This is yielding to the flow of the moment, not fighting it or trying to force it to what I wanted. I gave myself to the next 10 seconds, and in those moments, Onimusha soared. There are fights here – against Benkei, the Oni brothers, the Greater Nue, Ganryu, and several more I won’t spoil – that I will remember for a very long time. They would be excellent regardless, but by choosing to limit myself, I made the comebacks and the moments of perfection matter even more. Like Musashi, I put my belief in myself, in the strength of my technique and whatever I could carve from my opponent. Just when I thought it was impossible, I would find a way. My journey mirrored his.

Onimusha's bosses are its greatest strength, but its optional content is also strong. So strong, in fact, that I did all of its side missions (and everything else) over the course of my 39-hour playthrough. My favorites were quests from Lady Murasaki, a writer whose spirit stayed in the world of the living to tell stories. She would send me to get to the bottom of anything that seemed interesting so she could write about it, whether that was a child searching for a father consumed by revenge, a wife praying for her abusive husband's recovery, or a man who believed he had been blessed with immortality by the gods.

What's even better is that many of these side quests build upon one another, telling a single narrative across several smaller stories that Murasaki herself then records. Other side quests often don't feature the same level of detail (aside from Murasaki's and Shizuka’s, most side quests are not voiced), but using drawings to find hidden treasures scattered around Kyoto, returning to previous areas to shoot down flying Genma, or just helping average citizens is often funny and rewarding. Even hunting down and rescuing Murasaki’s missing Lion Dogs, a fairly normal take on collectibles, was entertaining because the dogs themselves were incredibly cute and each one also rewarded me with a retelling of a story from Japanese mythology. Some were funny, some were sad, and some were just plain weird, but I enjoyed reading them all. I also loved helping Shizuka find hidden Oni Portals scattered around the city, which illuminated more of her story and unlocked more tiers in my skill trees.

Onimusha's bosses are its greatest strength, but its side content is also strong.

I normally wouldn’t spill much ink over skill trees. In many games, the options locked within them feel like things you should have from the start that have only been taken away so that you have something to pursue; Onimusha, however, makes upgrades feel meaningful.

And it's not just skill trees. Equippable charms and stat upgrades provide an incentive to hunt down the upgrade items scattered around Kyoto and the other areas, which in turn made me want to explore the city, figure out workarounds to areas that had been blocked off, and open shortcuts once I did so I could get back there more easily. Every part of Onimusha touches every other part, and each piece is better for how it combines into a greater whole. Even something as simple as earning a new look for my sword or finding a new haori for Musashi to wear pointed to how far I’d come on my journey.

That all said, some minibosses such as the Byakue and Dohatsu-ten appear what feels like dozens of times across the main story and all of the sidequests, and certain main boss fights happen a few times as well. It’s a Capcom classic, but I was never bothered by these recursions; in fact, I often welcomed them. It was a chance to test my skills again, to gain greater mastery, to pit the Will and Musashi that were here now against those that had come before. Each time, I learned something. Each time, I sharpened my skills. That will be handy when I go back for another run in New Game plus or on Carnage, an additional difficulty you unlock after you complete the campaign. This time, though, I think I’ll let myself use items. Probably.

items.title: Lanterns Season 1, Episode 3 Review & Recap: 'OutKast'
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
Warning: This review contains full spoilers for

Lanterns sure does seem to enjoy hitting viewers with a big, last-minute twist and then immediately pivoting elsewhere in the following episode. The pilot culminated with a jump ahead to 2026 and the reveal that Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) has seemingly been murdered. Episode 2 avoided returning to the 2026 timeline at all, instead ending with circa-2016 Hal travelling to Oa and meeting with an incarcerated Sinestro (Ulrich Thomsen). And now our follow-up to that pivotal meeting is another jump backward, this time to the '80s and '90s for an installment that goes into great detail about John Stewart's peculiar origin story. That approach might almost be frustrating if not for the fact that the execution remains so strong. It turns out that this "mere" flashback episode is the best chapter of Lanterns to date.

Through its complex but easy-to-follow nonlinear narrative, Episode 3 fills in a great many blanks about John's childhood, his relationship with his parents, his doomed military career, and his recruitment into the Green Lantern Corps. It's interesting how little the series is actually drawing from the comics here. Trace elements remain, like John's mother being a formative influence and the Guardians keeping a watchful eye on him from afar, but for the most part, the show invents this origin story from whole cloth. It's a risk, but a very successful one.

Personally, I've about had my fill of superhero origin stories that center around a character grieving the loss of a parent figure and using that as propellant to become the hero they're destined to be. It's such a common trope in this genre, to the point where even Hal has a variation on that backstory. As such, I greatly appreciate how Lanterns tries to do something very different with John. He's not a plucky orphan. He's a kid whose parents are very much present and active in his upbringing, arguably to his detriment.

There's a very fun balance to the way John Sr. (J. Alphonse Nicholson) and Bernadette (Jasmine Cephas Jones) are depicted here. On one hand, they're shown to be strong, powerful role models for the impressionable young John Jr. (Cairo Cash Lee). Bernadette in particular serves as an eloquent voice for the show's racial themes, reminding both father and son repeatedly that they have to fight to be heard in a universe that doesn't value them. In a way, the show seems to be offering a more nuanced take on this well-meaning but very hamfisted scene from the Neal Adams/Denny O'Neil Green Lantern run:

On the other hand, these people are f***ing crazy. How do you justify repeatedly shooting apples off your son's head or dumping him to fend for himself on the bad side of Midway City? They're so wrapped up in the notion of their baby boy becoming a trailblazing superhero that they upend his life and raise him like a super-soldier in the making. Their singleminded obsession doesn't just border on child abuse, it is abuse, and it extends to their other sons as well. It's fascinating to watch two characters who are simultaneously so strong and committed and yet so fundamentally cruel. Again, it's such a refreshing change from the normal superhero tropes.

Both Nicholson and Cephas Jones are excellent throughout the episode, allowing us to see these characters as both human beings struggling to overcome adversity and oppressive tyrants in John's life. Parker especially gives us a very nuanced look into Bernadette's worldview and motivations. And. unsurprisingly, Aaron Pierre is a joy to watch in the later scenes focused on adult John. As I've said before, it's easy for a character this stoic and reserved to result in a boring performane, but Pierre is great at conveying all the emotional turmoil John silently wrestles with in his military career, his schooling, and his big interview.

On that note, this is where we also become acquainted with Laura Linney's character, one of the Guardians of Oa in human form. While a part of me wishes the series didn't always have to do this thing where it disguises its aliens as humans, Linney does an admirable job of playing a character who looks ordinary but is distinctly alien all the same. As with the John/Antaan (Paul Ben-Victor) scenes in Episode 2, the careful, purposeful dialogue choices open up a world of opportunity here.

In the end, what we're left with is a very clever, cohesive, and satisfying account of how an ordinary boy becomes groomed for the most important gig in the universe. In a more just world, John Stewart Jr. would have been left free to pursue his art and live life on his own terms. But with parents like these, you really have to take the cards you're dealt.

A few Easter eggs worth mentioning from this episode:

  • John's assassination target, Gray Wolf, is a minor character from DC's Batman Incorporated comics. It's always amusing to see the random bits of comic lore these DCU projects will mine.
  • There's a Janus Cosmetics poster in the background of the abandoned mall, referencing the company at the heart of the upcoming Clayface movie. It's another fun Batman-adjacent tidbit, and it does raise the question of whether Clayface is also taking place in the DCU's past (maybe to better justify the fact that Batman doesn't show up?).
  • It appears that John's childhood room has a sketch of Kilowog on the wall, which is probably the closest we'll get to seeing that particular Lantern in the show. It's interesting how much the average Earthling seems to know about the Green Lanterns in this universe. I guess it all speaks to the idea that metahumans are not a recent phenomenon in this world.

items.title: Fibbage Card Game Review
items.author: Jacob Kienlen
items.content:
All of the rules that have helped make this digital bluffing game have carried over to this new card game. As in the other iterations, in Fibbage one of the players will serve as a “revealer” who will draw a card and read aloud a prompt with a portion blanked out, and it is up to the other players to write down a plausible option to complete the prompt. However, the person who drew the prompt will have the correct answer and will write it down and add it as the correct answer. The players will all put in their answers, which will be shuffled, followed by a voting period where you vote for which you think is the right answer. From there, points are earned based on whether you guessed right and if others voted for your submission, and the person with the most points at the end of however many rounds you decide on (by default it’s six rounds) wins.

Inside the box, which is roughly the size of a standard hardcover book, the rules are on a single side of paper (the other side is an ad for Jackbox Party Pack 4), cardboard voting/point tokens (but strangely no bag to put them in), six dry-erase markers with boards, and 300 cards with prompts. The prompts themselves span an eclectic range of topics, from asking about chefs who cook ducks with hair dryers to Japan-exclusive flavors of Pepsi. The impressive number of cards means you will have a good number of games to get through before you start getting many repeats, which is great.

The Fibbage Card Game, just like the digital version, is ripe for expansion after expansion, and knowing Jackbox, I imagine it won’t be long until we start seeing packs of additional prompt cards, different themed prompts, and extra markers and boards to write on. There really isn’t any reason that you can’t expand the player count to as high as you want, so long as you have things to write with and on, and something to keep track of the points with.

"Fibbage ranks up there as one of my favorite purely party games out there. It's one of those games that even ol’ grandma and grandpa can get in on and have a good time with."

Everything about Fibbage has made the jump to a physical game rather successfully, with one slight exception - the writing the answer part. Does it work? Sure. The issue is that considering the revealer knows that answer, unless your group has really similar handwriting, or at least writing box letters similarly (which the game suggests you use), before too long you will probably start recognizing the handwriting of the players. Especially in lower player count games. A situation I ran into.

A bit of homebrew magic I worked out was that I had the revealer gather the submissions, then, on a separate sheet of paper, copy down all the answers, and the group would vote on that list. It does add an extra step and a little more time, but this does manage to keep the votes tied to the answer as opposed to everyone pretending they are a forensic document examiner (I looked that one up; an FDE looks at and compares handwriting and signatures for the court - also may or may not be a question on one of the cards).

Regardless of how you play it, Fibbage ranks up there as one of my favorite purely party games out there. It's one of those games that even ol’ grandma and grandpa can get in on and have a good time with. I’ve always appreciated the fact that Fibbage asks a bit more of its players, requiring you to be a bit more clever and creative without relying so much on “who has the funniest response” to score points. An outcome that I’ve found games of Cards Against Humanity and others tend to devolve into. This physical version of Fibbage is a really faithful adaptation of a game with a proven track record of being a hit at parties, and one I can see myself bringing out frequently.

items.title: Gandahar Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
The new 4K restoration of the uncut French version of Gandahar is being released in New York City on August 28 before expanding nationally.

Man, who remembers the crop of great, strange, watch ’em in your buddy’s finished basement (probably after a couple of bong hits) animated classics like , Fantastic Planet, , and the such? Pre-internet, popping these movies into your VHS or DVD player was like playing the freak-out lottery: What weird and wonderful delights awaited you were anyone’s guess.

And now, Janus Films has unleashed a new 4K restoration of one such title, the late French animator René Laloux’s Gandahar. Laloux was also the mind behind 1973’s better-remembered cult classic (aka La Planète Sauvage). Like that film, 1987’s Gandahar is a trippy (I promise not to use that word again in this review) visit to a far-out realm, only in this case it’s a land where soulless robots attempt to overtake a seemingly utopian society, and the battle for freedom must be fought not just in the here and now, but also 1,000 years in the future. Along the way, the dangers of genetic experiments, the consequences of creating an ultimate weapon, and the effect such decisions have on future generations are all explored. Also, clothing is optional for half of these characters (the female half, as was the wont of the time).

An edited and dubbed version of the film called was released in North America by (cough) Miramax Films in 1988. That cut even featured dialogue written by legendary sci-fi scribe Isaac Asimov, who adapted the French script, but now Janus has given us the complete and original version of the sci-fi adventure. And really, the steady (sometimes somnambulistic by today’s standards) pace, the heady visuals and concepts, and the French line readings make an English version of Gandahar – voiced by the likes of John Shea, Jennifer Grey and Christopher Plummer, as Light Years apparently was – just seem wrong.

It’s the weirdos and oddballs that Gandahar is all about.

The film begins with scenes of bucolic, if strange, beauty, as a group of blue-skinned villagers fish and eat and play. An anteater-type creature is born from a plant, and immediately the babe suckles at a woman’s chest as if she’s its mother. (Maybe she is?) Birds peck at giant berries while the villagers collect them, giant snails feed while a shepherd looks on, but then suddenly… an attack! The people of Gandahar are being turned to stone by the C-3PO-like (only mean, and black) Men of Metal.

And so in the city of Jasper (which is centered in a giant statue of a woman) the leader of the Council of Women (who has huge eagle wings sticking out of the sides of her head) is advised by her lead scientist (who looks like he’s come straight out of the Green Lanterns’ Guardians of the Universe) to send out an emissary to investigate the situation. (And yes, I could keep inserting parentheticals around just about every noun in this movie to explain some kind of weirdness, which is half the film’s charm right there.)

The young “Servant” Sylvain (voiced by Pierre-Marie Escourrou) is put on the case, and while the character hits his marks as a hero – he rides a flying, flapping, funky mechanical jellyfish; shoots a gun that uses ammo which quickly propagates as spiky weeds; gets the girl; and saves the day – he’s also dry as the desert landscape where that jellyfish crash-lands. Alas, none of the human characters in this tale are particularly engaging, but that’s OK because it’s the weirdos and oddballs that Gandahar is all about.

Take the Deformed, the outcasts of Gandahar who are the result of scientific experimentation – “victims of your genetic games,” they tell Sylvain – and as such have all manner of physicality, from multiple heads to mouths for knees to my favorite, the dude who is a huge head/chest with arms that he walks on. Also blessed/cursed with the ability to see the future, only to lose it, the Deformed now speak in the past and future tense because that’s how they see the world around them: In 1,000 years, Gandahar has fallen. 1,000 years ago, Gandahar will be saved.

Then there’s Metamorphis (Georges Wilson), a giant brain hanging out in the middle of the Eccentric Ocean, as it is rightfully called. Another forgotten legacy of Gandahar, Metamorphis is either the villain of the film or its hero, depending on your point of view. But that’s the thing about Gandahar the movie – just as its imagery is off-kilter but also beautiful, its loopy time-travel story isn’t terribly interested in adhering to traditional concepts of what an animated film needs to be. So yes, sometimes it’s slow, sometimes its hero is kind of lame, and sometimes it’s rough around the edges. But just like Fantastic Planet before it, it’s not the kind of thing that passes for big-screen animation these days, and that kind of makes it a must-watch right there. (Pass the bong.)

items.title: NBA 2K27 Review
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
Just like our favorite NBA teams, the NBA 2K series teases enough improvements every year to give us a sliver of hope; a renewed sense of faith that maybe things will be even better than last time. Although that faith was rewarded for NBA 2K26, that hasn’t been the case with NBA 2K27. While the on-court play does feel better thanks to smoother and more responsive defensive movements, some new additions, like MyCareer Eras and MyNBA Legacy, are the opposite. Instead, they act like magnifiers, placing a spotlight on issues that have consistently plagued this series, like an ever-growing emphasis on microtransactions and half-baked features. That can turn what should be an energizing session of hoops into a tiring exercise in scrutiny.

Let’s kick things off with the good stuff: the on-court experience. Offense, although it still feels largely the same, has a few new tricks up its sleeve that make it slightly more challenging than last year. For starters, Rhythm Shooting is much less forgiving than in 2K26 since you’ll have to actually hit the green part of your shot meter to make jumpers. Full disclosure: I religiously use the square button to shoot because it’s what I’ve been doing since 2K10. With this change, I've become even more partial to the classic hold-and-release method since there just doesn’t seem to be an incentive to master Rhythm Shooting’s more finicky timing and down-up motion. Of course, there may come a point when I’ll need to really dig into the latter, but today is not that day.

Then there’s the new logic-based Dunk Meter, which, instead of only showing up when you perform Skill Dunks like in 2K26, now appears whenever you drive to and attempt a shot at the rim. The goal, as always, is to hit the green, but it won’t always be that simple, because this feature takes the defender’s positioning into account. That means even if you get a near-perfect release on your way to a jam, a well-timed contest from a towering, highly-rated defender like Zach Edey or Victor Wembanyama could turn it into a miss.

I’ll admit, taking the Dunk Meter into account did take some getting used to, meaning I’ve missed more than a few slams in trying to master it. But I eventually came to appreciate the greater sense of realism it lends to 2K27. As much as I would want every poster dunk attempt to go in, even a strong and sure-handed player like Giannis can and should get stuffed at the rim every now and then.

This, of course, leads me to the side of the ball that flusters dribblers, causes turnovers, and wins championships. If last year’s defense was a benchwarmer who barely played any minutes, this year it’s the Most Improved Player. As soon as I hopped into a match, the change felt immediate; being near a defender and putting a hand up actually altered a shot! Gone are the dark days when every jumper, even contested ones, felt like they would go in; now that both sides of the ball are balanced, playing through an entire game in both online and offline modes feels better and more competitive than ever.

If 2K26’s defense was a benchwarmer, 2k27's is the Most Improved Player.

That includes contests in the newest space where all the cool kids in The City hangout: Casual Corner. This place has almost everything: 3v3, 5v5, PvE and PvP games, you name it. But fair warning; this is not a place to let your guard down. The more you play here (or in any other mode, for that matter), the more you’ll be matched with higher skill players. After all, the main purpose of this spot is to train beginners and ease them into high stakes match types like Ante Up or Proving Grounds.

Although the wins I racked up in Casual Corner didn’t feel as rewarding as those in, say, The Theater, it’s often a better and more relaxed alternative. I mean, there are only so many ballhogs and non-passers I can take before steam starts coming out my ears, making this a great place to reset or, at the very least, get some runs in without having to worry about losses.

Now, if you ever wonder why you just got crossed up by a flash of long lashes and a top bun, it’s because The City is now co-ed! That’s right; you can now create female players who can then represent you in the bustling hub as you roam around or play through online matches. Want to know what’s even better? There are no downsides to making female builds. On the court, it’s still all about skill, the way it should be, so excuse me while I take some scrubs to school with my sharpshooting Kayla McBride archetype.

It’s time to head on over to MyCareer’s neck of the woods, with its latest single-player journey, dramatically titled Fire and Concrete. Like always, this tale follows our recurring hero MP, showing his hoops growth in stages from humble high school roots all the way to a career in the pros. Unlike its predecessors, though, this one’s a doozy, spanning 11 chapters – and bigger always means better, right? Oh, if only that were true.

As soon as I jumped into the thick of things, some flaws immediately stood out, beginning with the story itself. Early on, a key plot point is rushed through in an animated vignette instead of actually unfolding in a full cutscene – it was more like watching a commercial than a career-defining incident. It flashed by so fast that I almost missed it, and that makes the start of MP’s journey, arguably the most important part, feel like an afterthought.

Then, there’s MP himself, who is hard to root for. Although he does become less of a diva as the story progresses, he’s still often outshined by the supporting characters throughout, like his funny cousin Cam, who is voiced and mocapped by Vince Staples. Even Cade Cunningham, who only had a bit part during the story’s G-League portion, had more presence than him. Overall, it’s like every drop of personality has been sucked out of this MP and given to those around him, which is a step back from the endearing (albeit overenthusiastic) version from 2K26.

As soon as I jumped into MyCareer, some flaws immediately stood out.

The bad news doesn’t stop there, because as underwhelming as 2K27’s hoops tale is, one new MyCareer feature has been even more disappointing: the dynamic draft board. Unlike last year, which saw you get drafted at a fixed position to a team of your choice, you can actually move up and down the list this year based on your performance. This sounded great at first; I loved that it gave me a sense of progress after each match. But that only lasted until I reached the draft itself; once I did, I found out I could just choose which team I want to play for, and that made the whole thing feel pointless.

Luckily, it’s not all missed shots and Shaqtin-a-Fool blooper reels in this middling basketball tale. There is one bright spot I’ve saved for last: the new Running Mate co-op feature. As the name implies, this gives you a hoop partner who’ll always be there to provide screens and catch your badly timed alley-oops no matter what.
